body: A safety-dashboard is a visual interface that aggregates safety metrics, indicators, and operational data into a single display surface for situational awareness and decision-making. It is carved by its visual (non-textual) presentation of multiple safety data sources, its real-time or near-real-time refresh capability, and its role as a decision-support tool rather than a data collection mechanism itself. It persists through software implementation and operational maintenance in the matter substrate. [formal: tabula visualis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety signoff is a formal, documented authorization gate where designated individuals or committees certify that all applicable safety requirements, inspections, and test results for a given phase or product have been satisfied, thereby permitting progression to the next development or operational stage. Its parameters are: (1) a designated authority with the competence and mandate to assess safety compliance, (2) a defined checklist of safety requirements that must be verified, (3) a recorded decision (approved or rejected) with justification, and (4) a binding effect — work cannot proceed past the gate without affirmative signoff. It persists through audit trails, signed documents, and regulatory databases. [formal: sigillum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An incident report is a human-made documentation artifact that records the details of a safety-relevant event: what happened, when and where it occurred, who was involved, what immediate causes and contributing factors were identified, and what corrective or preventive actions were taken or recommended. It persists through formal record-keeping systems maintained by organizations for regulatory compliance, learning, and accountability. [formal: relatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety metrics are human-made measurement instruments: quantified indicators collected, calculated, and reported to assess the state of safety performance within an organization. They include lagging indicators (incident rates, lost-time injury frequency) and leading indicators (safety training completion rates, audit findings resolved, hazard reports filed). They persist through systematic data collection, analysis, and reporting processes built into organizational information systems. [formal: mensura | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A safety control is a human-made measure, device, or procedure deployed to eliminate, reduce, or mitigate a hazard to an acceptable level. Its parameters are: (1) the hazard or risk it addresses, (2) the mechanism of control (engineering, administrative, or personal protective), and (3) the performance criteria that determine whether it is effective. A safety control persists through institutional implementation — embedded in organizational procedures, physical infrastructure, or technological systems — and is maintained through audits, reviews, and corrective actions. [formal: praesidium securitatis | substrate: behavior|matter | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety target is a human-made, measurable goal established by an organization to reduce risk or improve safety performance over a defined period. Its parameters are: (1) the specific hazard or performance area it addresses, (2) the quantifiable metric and threshold that define success, (3) the timeframe for achievement, and (4) the organizational unit responsible for delivery. Safety targets are derived from hazard assessments, regulatory requirements, and prior performance data; they translate broad safety objectives into actionable, trackable commitments. They persist through formal documentation, management review cycles, and organizational reporting systems. [formal: finis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

Safety-monitoring is a human-made system of observation and measurement designed to track safety performance indicators, detect hazards, and verify compliance. Its parameters are: (1) the metrics and indicators selected for tracking (e.g. incident rates, exposure levels, compliance percentages), (2) the instruments and methods used to collect data (sensors, inspections, audits, reporting systems), and (3) the feedback loop that translates observed data into actionable corrections. [formal: monitoring | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.12]

A safety-knowledge-base is a structured repository system that captures, organizes, and provides access to safety-related information — procedures, incident reports, risk assessments, lessons learned, and best practices — maintained by organizational safety teams. It persists through digital document management with version control, metadata tagging, and search indexing; its structure organizes knowledge into categories of procedural, incident-based, preventive, and corrective information. Retrieval occurs through query interfaces and structured browsing, enabling continuity of safety practice across personnel changes and organizational time. [formal: basilica-notionum-salutarium | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-simulation is a modeling technique that reproduces system conditions — operational, fault, or emergency — in a controlled environment to examine how safety behaviors manifest, test responses, and predict failure modes. It operates by creating representative scenarios, observing system reactions, and extracting safety-relevant insights without exposing real assets to risk. [formal: simulatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-maturity-model is a human-made framework that stages the evolution of organizational safety capabilities across a sequence of levels, each describing progressively more disciplined and integrated practices for identifying, assessing, and controlling hazards. It carves a progression path — from ad hoc reactive responses at the lowest level to optimized, continuously improving safety culture at the highest — and persists through formal assessment instruments, audit checklists, and organizational self-evaluation protocols that map current practice against the staged benchmark. [formal: maturitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-assurance is a human-made institutional practice that verifies and validates that safety measures are functioning as designed and that required safety standards are being met. It carves a closed-loop process: establishing safety performance indicators, monitoring compliance against those indicators, auditing and inspecting to detect deviations, and implementing corrective actions to restore conformity. It persists through scheduled audits, compliance reporting systems, management review cycles, and corrective-action tracking databases that close the feedback loop between verification and improvement. [formal: securitas assumpta | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-resilience is the engineered capacity of safety systems and organizational processes to absorb operational disturbances, adapt to emerging threats, and recover essential safety functions after disruptions. It is distinguished from static safety measures by its emphasis on adaptive response, learning under stress, and functional recovery rather than prevention alone. Its parameters are: (1) the range of disturbances it can absorb (vulnerability threshold), (2) the speed and completeness of functional recovery (recovery time objective), and (3) the mechanisms of adaptive learning that update safety practices post-event. It persists through organizational routines — debrief protocols, adaptive training exercises, and documented lessons-learned systems — embedded in institutional memory and reinforced by management review cycles. [formal: resilientia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-testing is a human-made verification practice that exercises safety-critical systems or processes under controlled conditions to confirm they meet specified safety requirements before deployment or during operational life. It operates by generating empirical evidence of safety performance through structured test scenarios — including fault injection, boundary testing, and stress testing — that map to the safety requirements derived from hazard assessments. The mechanism of persistence is the test artifact (plans, procedures, results, traceability matrices) that is reviewed, audited, and updated as requirements evolve through the product lifecycle. [formal: probatio experimentalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.58]

Safety-readiness is a human-made organizational assessment practice that evaluates whether personnel, procedures, equipment, and systems are adequately prepared to execute safety functions under expected and unexpected operating conditions. It operates by measuring the gap between current preparedness levels and defined readiness criteria through audits, drills, tabletop exercises, and capability gap analyses. The mechanism of persistence is the readiness posture — a maintained state of trained personnel, calibrated equipment, validated procedures, and documented procedures that is periodically reassessed and updated through scheduled readiness reviews and continuous improvement cycles. [formal: aptitudo securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.59]

Safety-compliance is a human-made governance practice that verifies organizational processes, systems, and behaviors conform to established safety requirements, standards, and regulations. It operates through structured audit cycles that compare actual practice against codified requirements, produces documentary evidence of conformity (or non-conformity), and triggers corrective action when gaps are identified. Its persistence mechanism is institutionalized audit protocols maintained by compliance officers and external regulators, with records retained for regulatory review and continuous improvement. [formal: compliantia | substrate: behavior | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

Safety planning is the structured, forward-looking process of establishing safety objectives, identifying potential hazards, and designing controls before operational work commences. It produces documented plans, procedures, and frameworks that specify how risks will be managed, who is responsible for safety actions, and what resources will be allocated. Safety planning operates at the strategic and tactical levels: at strategic level it sets the safety policy and priorities; at tactical level it develops specific action plans for known hazards. The persistence mechanism is institutional documentation — written plans, standard operating procedures, and organizational charters that are reviewed, updated, and enforced over time. [formal: prudentia practica | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.13]

A safety-maturity model is a human-made framework for evaluating and classifying the sophistication, integration, and continuous improvement of an organization's safety management practices across defined levels of development. It provides structured criteria and assessment scales that enable organizations to benchmark their safety culture and practices against standardized benchmarks, identify gaps in their safety systems, and prioritize investment in safety capabilities. The framework persists through standardized rubrics, assessment protocols, and reporting mechanisms used by safety professionals to guide organizational learning and systematic improvement. [formal: maturitas | substrate: mind | horizon: years | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-lapse is a human-made categorization of a specific type of safety-incident in which safety controls are breached through failure, omission, or error, resulting in increased risk exposure. It is distinguished from near-misses (where no actual harm occurs) and from intentional violations: a lapse is unintentional — a gap between intended and actual safety performance that manifests as a real incident. The concept enables organizations to classify incidents by control-failure mode, identify systematic weaknesses in safety barriers, and design targeted interventions. [formal: lapsus | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-recovery is a human-made categorization of the coordinated processes activated after a safety incident to restore normal operations, mitigate damage, and stabilize affected systems and personnel. Its parameters include: (1) triggering conditions (incident severity thresholds, operational impact criteria), (2) response phase (immediate stabilization, recovery execution, return-to-normal), (3) responsible actors (incident commanders, recovery teams, subject-matter experts), and (4) success criteria (restored function, reduced risk to baseline). It persists through documented recovery plans, trained response teams, exercised procedures, and post-incident after-action reviews. [formal: recuperatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-signaling is a human-made mechanism — a visual, auditory, digital, or procedural cue — designed to communicate safety-relevant information (hazard presence, system status, required action, or boundary conditions) to observers within a system's operating environment. It persists through standardized formats (colors, symbols, alarms, indicators), institutionalized protocols (lockout-tagout, emergency codes), and embedded device behavior (warning lights, proximity alerts). Safety signals are engineered for recognizability under stress, differentiated from non-safety information, and calibrated to avoid desensitization through controlled frequency and intensity. They operate as pre-cognitive triggers that compress complex risk assessment into immediate behavioral guidance. [formal: signum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-risk is the concept of a hazard or peril scoped to the safety domain: a combination of the likelihood and severity of harm to people, property, or the environment. It is the primary object of risk assessment and risk management processes, serving as the unit of analysis when evaluating whether a given situation, process, or artifact presents unacceptable danger. Safety-risk is distinguished from general risk by its focus on harm to living systems and critical infrastructure, not merely financial, operational, or strategic loss. [formal: periculum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-investigation is the practice of examining incidents, accidents, and near-misses after they occur to determine root causes and generate lessons learned. It operates through formal investigation procedures, root-cause analysis methods (such as fault-tree analysis, 5-whys, and barrier analysis), and institutional reporting systems that capture findings for preventive action. The practice persists through documented investigation protocols, trained investigators, and feedback loops that convert findings into corrective and preventive actions. [formal: investigatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

A safety-incident is a human-made classification of an event that has actual or potential to cause harm to people, property, or the environment. It is a constructed category used in occupational health and safety management systems to record, track, and learn from events that disrupted or could have disrupted safe operations. Safety-incidents are classified by severity, type, and outcome (near-miss, minor injury, major accident), and persist through formal reporting systems, databases, and regulatory records. [formal: incidentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-traceability is a human-made system for maintaining a documented, unbroken chain of evidence linking safety-related decisions, actions, and outcomes back to their requirements, sources, and justifications. It is a constructed information-management practice that ensures every safety conclusion can be traced to its data inputs, analytical methods, and review approvals. Safety-traceability persists through documentation trails, audit logs, and traceability matrices used in safety-critical industries. [formal: tractabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-architecture is a human-made framework that structures safety controls, governance arrangements, and compliance requirements into an integrated design spanning system engineering and organizational management. It carves the relationship between safety objectives, their allocation across system layers, and the verification mechanisms that ensure requirements propagate from top-level policies to individual components. The framework persists through engineering standards (ISO 26262, DO-178C, IEC 61508), safety case methodologies (Goal Structuring Notation), and regulatory compliance architectures that formalize its structure and govern its evolution across product lifecycles. [formal: architectura salutis | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

Safety-integration is the practice of embedding safety considerations into the design, operations, planning, and decision-making processes of an organization or system, so that safety becomes a constitutive element of all activities rather than a separate compliance silo. It operates through organizational structures, standard procedures, training programs, and cultural norms that weave safety analysis into engineering, procurement, production, and management workflows. The persistence mechanism is institutional: embedded in roles, checklists, review gates, and the routine deliberations of those who design and operate systems. [formal: formalisatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.11]

A structured process framework that sequences safety-relevant activities across the stages of a system's existence — conception, design, implementation, operation, maintenance, and decommissioning — so that hazards are identified, risks are assessed and treated, and safety performance is verified and reviewed at each stage. Its parameters are the stage boundary (which defines which safety activities apply), the feedback loop (which carries lessons from operation back to design), and the governance checkpoint (which authorizes progression to the next stage). It persists through documented procedures, standardized templates, and regulatory or organizational mandates that require compliance audits. [formal: lifecycle | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-goals are human-made constructs: a structured set of objectives, derived from risk assessments and management commitments, that define the desired state of safety performance within an organization. The parameters that bound this concept are: (1) they must be derived from systematic risk evaluation, (2) they must be communicated across organizational levels, and (3) they must be subject to periodic review and revision. The mechanism by which they persist is organizational documentation — policy statements, safety management system manuals, regulatory filings, and audit records — reinforced through repeated managerial practice and external certification requirements. Without this documented persistence, safety-goals would collapse into informal intentions rather than operating as a stable construct.\n\n[formal: finis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-instruction is the human-made practice of delivering focused, task-relevant safety knowledge to individuals or teams before or during work. Its parameters are: (1) audience specificity — directed at people about to perform or currently performing particular tasks; (2) temporal proximity — delivered immediately before or during the relevant activity; (3) content specificity — covers particular hazards, controls, and procedures for the task at hand, not general safety awareness; (4) format brevity — typically short, verbal or visual, designed for immediate comprehension and application. It persists through documented briefings, checklists, posted procedures, and oral tradition in shift-based work. Safety-instruction differs from safety-training (broader, curriculum-based, often periodic) in its just-in-time, task-embedded character. [formal: instructio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety performance is a quantifiable measure of how effectively an organization's safety management system prevents harm and controls risk. Its parameters include leading indicators (proactive measures such as training completion rates, inspection frequencies, hazard identification counts) and lagging indicators (reactive measures such as incident rates, severity scores, regulatory non-compliance events). The construct persists through institutional reporting systems, regulatory frameworks, benchmarking practices, and continuous improvement cycles that institutionalize the measurement of safety outcomes. [formal: de excellentia securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.31]

A safety-briefing is a timed, face-to-face or virtual gathering in which a supervisor or safety representative communicates task-specific hazards, required controls, and emergency procedures to workers before they begin work. It is characterized by (1) a fixed agenda covering hazards, controls, and procedures; (2) attendance by all personnel affected by the work; (3) a documented record of what was communicated. It persists through scheduled recurrence, standardized templates, and organizational practice rather than through any single document.

A safety-accountability mechanism assigns specific safety responsibilities to defined roles within an organization and establishes formal processes for reporting, review, and consequence when safety outcomes deviate from expectations. It persists through written charters, job descriptions, performance metrics, and audit trails that record who is responsible for what. The mechanism operates as a designed structure of answerability — distinct from moral guilt, it is the procedural obligation to explain and justify safety-related decisions and outcomes to designated authorities. [formal: responsabilitas | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.42]

A KPI is a quantifiable metric selected to track and assess progress toward specific organizational or individual objectives. It is distinguished from ordinary metrics by its direct linkage to a defined goal and its use in decision-making: a KPI answers whether a particular objective is being met, and its value is reviewed on a regular cycle (daily, weekly, monthly) by stakeholders who act on the results. Its parameters are: (1) a numeric or categorical value, (2) an associated objective it measures against, (3) a reporting frequency, and (4) an assigned owner accountable for the result. It persists through formal reporting frameworks, management software, and the shared vocabulary of organizational practice — embedded in dashboards, board reports, and performance reviews.\n\n[formal: kpi | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Incident reporting is a formalized procedure that requires individuals to document workplace incidents, near-misses, and hazardous conditions using standardized forms or digital systems, then route those reports through a defined chain of review and response. Its parameters are: (1) the event must be work-related (occupational injury, illness, property damage, or near-miss), (2) reporting follows prescribed templates that capture what happened, where, when, and who was involved, and (3) reports trigger investigation and corrective action. It persists through codified organizational policies, regulatory mandates (e.g., OSHA recordkeeping), and the institutional memory of aggregated report databases that feed preventive improvement. [formal: relatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-failure is the occurrence of a harm or near-harm event within a system, arising from the breakdown of safety measures, controls, or protocols designed to prevent it. It is the concrete instantiation of a safety gap: when a identified risk materializes, or when a latent defect in procedures, equipment, or human judgment produces an adverse outcome. Parameters: (1) it must occur within a human-made system (industrial, organizational, infrastructural, or digital); (2) it involves actual or imminent harm to persons, property, or function; (3) it traces to a failure of some safety mechanism that existed or should have existed. Persistence mechanism: safety-failures are recorded in incident databases, reported through safety-reporting systems, and analyzed in post-incident reviews — the concept persists through systematic documentation, regulatory reporting, and organizational learning. [formal: failure_of_safety | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.62]

A safety-gate is a formal decision point embedded within a project or product development lifecycle, where compliance with specified safety criteria is evaluated and a documented go/no-go ruling is issued before the project may advance to the next stage. Its parameters are: (1) the lifecycle stage at which it occurs, (2) the safety criteria against which compliance is measured, (3) the decision authority vested in the gatekeepers, and (4) the documented outcome that either authorizes or blocks progression. It persists through governance frameworks, regulatory mandates, and organizational procedure manuals that institutionalize the practice of verifying safety at critical junctures rather than attempting to retrofit it after the fact. [formal: transitus | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A flow diagram is a visual representation that maps the sequence of operations, decision points, and data or material movements within a process. It uses standardized symbols—ovals for start/end points, rectangles for processes, diamonds for decisions, and directed arrows for flow—to show how information, materials, or control passes through a system. The persistence mechanism is visual documentation standards (ISO 5807, ANSI Y14.00) and diagramming software, enabling reproduction, sharing, and updating across organizational boundaries. A flow diagram extends human capacity for tracking multi-step processes beyond working memory limits, serving as both a planning artifact and an operational reference. [formal: flowus diagramma | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-program is a structured organizational framework that integrates policies, procedures, training, and continuous improvement mechanisms to systematically manage workplace hazards and reduce risk. It establishes accountability, sets measurable objectives, and sustains safety performance through documented processes and regular review cycles. [formal: program | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-integrity is the quantified trust that a safety-related system (hardware, software, or both) will perform its required safety functions correctly on demand and within a specified performance level. It is characterized by measurable targets such as Safety Integrity Levels (SIL 1–4) or Performance Levels (PL a–e), defined by the probability of dangerous failure per hour (PFHd) or average time to dangerous failure (TFHd). Its persistence is maintained through standardization (IEC 61508 for general industry, IEC 61511 for process sectors, ISO 13849 for machinery), third-party certification, periodic functional safety assessments, and lifecycle verification from design through decommissioning. [formal: integritas securitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

Safety-significance is a classification framework that assigns importance levels to components, failure modes, or processes based on their potential impact on system safety. Its parameters are (1) consequence severity — the harm that could result from a failure, graded from negligible to catastrophic, and (2) likelihood or availability of the failure — how frequently or under what conditions it may occur. These parameters map to standardized classification tiers such as Safety Integrity Levels (SIL 1–4) in IEC 61508 or Automotive Safety Integrity Levels (ASIL A–D) in ISO 26262. The framework persists through safety cases — structured, evidence-supported arguments for the adequacy of safety measures — and through certification documents produced during regulatory review. It enables consistent allocation of verification rigor proportional to risk across engineering disciplines. [formal: safety-significantia | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.27]

Safety-culture-assessment is a systematic evaluation instrument that diagnoses the shared attitudes, beliefs, values, and behavioral norms regarding safety within an organization. Its parameters are (1) dimension measured — leadership commitment, worker participation, reporting willingness, or learning orientation; (2) method — structured survey, semi-structured interview, direct observation, or documentary analysis; (3) scoring — normalized scale enabling intra-organizational comparison and inter-temporal trend tracking. It persists through standardized instruments, periodic administration, and documented results that inform safety-management interventions. [formal: culturae securitatis aestimatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-leading-indicator is a proactive measurement construct that quantifies preventive safety activities and conditions to predict and prevent harm before it occurs. Its parameters are (1) activity type — training, inspection, observation, or reporting; (2) frequency — daily, weekly, or monthly collection; (3) threshold — the target value that signals adequate preventive effort. It persists through safety management systems and regulatory reporting frameworks. [formal: indicium principale | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-trailing-indicator is a retrospective measurement construct that quantifies actual harm events, near-misses, and safety failures after they occur to evaluate past safety performance. Its parameters are (1) event type — recordable incidents, lost-time injuries, property damage, near-misses; (2) aggregation period — monthly, quarterly, annual reporting cycles; and (3) normalization — incidents per hours worked, per production unit, or per operational cycle. It persists through incident tracking systems, regulatory reporting databases, and organizational safety records. [formal: indicium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Hazard communication is a structured system for conveying safety-relevant information about dangerous substances, conditions, and practices to persons who may be exposed. Its parameters are (1) the hazard identity — chemical, physical, or biological — (2) the transmission medium — labels, data sheets, posted signs, training sessions, or digital alerts — and (3) the required content — nature of hazard, protective measures, and emergency procedures. It persists through institutionalized documentation, regulatory requirement, and ongoing re-education cycles. [formal: communicatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A human-made system for conveying safety-relevant information about dangerous substances, conditions, and practices to persons who may be exposed. Its parameters are (1) the hazard identity (chemical, physical, biological), (2) the audience (workers, responders, general public), (3) the medium (labels, safety data sheets, oral warnings, training, pictograms), and (4) the regulatory framework governing disclosure. It persists through standardized documentation, regulatory mandates, and organizational communication protocols. [formal: communicatio_periculi | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-goal is a broadly framed, high-level aim for the safety performance of an organization or system. Its parameters are (1) the domain of application (the operational context the goal applies to), (2) the safety outcome it targets (the class of harm or loss it seeks to prevent), and (3) the level of aspiration (the standard of performance the goal sets). It persists through formal documentation in safety management systems — typically safety policies, strategic plans, and governance frameworks — and endures across organizational cycles because it defines direction rather than method. [formal: scopulus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A hazard communication is a structured system for identifying, documenting, and conveying safety-relevant information about dangerous substances, conditions, and practices to persons who may be exposed to them. Its parameters are: (1) the hazard source (substance, condition, or practice), (2) the audience (those potentially exposed), (3) the medium (labels, data sheets, training, signage, alerts), and (4) the content (nature of danger, precautions, emergency measures). It persists through institutional enforcement — regulations such as OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard, employer-mandated programs, and standardized formats (SDS sheets, GHS labels) that are taught, audited, and updated whenever new hazards are identified. Without these standardized channels, hazard information disperses into noise and fails to reach the people who need it.\n[formal: communicatio_periculorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-criterion is a formally established standard, benchmark, or requirement that specifies acceptable levels of safety performance, conditions, or controls. It defines the measurable parameters against which safety systems, processes, or outcomes are evaluated. Safety-criteria are produced by regulatory bodies, industry standards organizations, and organizational safety management systems; they persist through codification in regulations, standards documents, and organizational policies, and are updated through formal revision processes. [formal: criterion | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hazard communication is the structured conveyance of information about dangers, risks, and unsafe conditions to workers, the public, or any audience that must understand and act on that information. It encompasses labels, safety data sheets (SDS), warning signs, training programs, and written procedures — each a formalized carrier of hazard knowledge. Parameters: (1) the information must identify a specific hazard and its control measures; (2) the medium must be standardized enough for cross-context comprehension (GHS labels, SDS formats, signal words); (3) the audience must include anyone who could be exposed. Persistence mechanism: regulatory frameworks (OSHA HazCom 2012, UN GHS), organizational SOPs, and legally mandated training curricula that encode and reproduce the communication across time and institutional boundaries. The map persists through codified standards and institutional enforcement — without them the concept dissolves into informal warning. [formal: nuntiatio_periculi | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-protocol is a codified set of procedures, rules, and behavioral requirements designed to prevent, mitigate, or manage safety risks in a specific operational context. It specifies required actions, prohibitions, equipment standards, and response sequences that must be followed to maintain safety integrity. It persists through written documentation, organizational enforcement, training regimens, and audit mechanisms that ensure compliance across operational lifecycles. [formal: protocolium securitatis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-standard is a formally documented set of requirements, guidelines, or characteristics for safety-related products, processes, systems, or practices. It is defined by its scope of application, mandatory versus advisory provisions, compliance criteria, and revision history. Safety-standards persist through publication in standards catalogs, regulatory codification, and organizational adoption. [formal: norma | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.43]

A safety-checklist is a structured, enumerated list of items, steps, or verification points designed to ensure that safety procedures are completed correctly and consistently. It is defined by its composition (ordered or categorized items), its scope of application (specific task, phase, or operation), and its persistence mechanism (documented in standard operating procedures, training materials, or digital checklists). [formal: lista | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hazard communication is a structured system for conveying information about dangerous substances, conditions, and practices to persons who may be exposed. It is defined by its regulated format (labels, safety data sheets, training programs), its mandated scope (all hazardous materials within an organization or jurisdiction), and its two-way flow: upward reporting of incidents alongside downward distribution of precautions. It persists through written procedures, posted labels, documented training records, and regulatory enforcement — institutionalized in standards such as OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) and the Globally Harmonized System (GHS). [formal: periculo-communicatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hazard communication is a structured system for conveying information about dangerous substances, conditions, and practices to persons who may be exposed. It is defined by its regulated format (labels, safety data sheets, training programs), its mandated scope (all hazardous materials within an organization or jurisdiction), and its two-way flow: upward reporting of incidents alongside downward distribution of precautions. It persists through written procedures, posted labels, documented training records, and regulatory enforcement — institutionalized in standards such as OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (29 CFR 1910.1200) and the Globally Harmonized System (GHS). [formal: periculo-communicatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A training is a structured program of instruction designed to develop competencies in a specific domain. It is defined by its curriculum (content sequenced for progressive learning), its methodology (pedagogical approach matched to subject matter), and its assessment mechanism (measures of competency gain). Training persists through institutional practice, documented curricula, and the reproduction of teaching relationships between instructor and learner. [formal: institutio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-participation is a structured mechanism for involving workers in the identification of hazards, the development of safety rules, and the evaluation of safety performance. It is defined by its formal channels (safety committees, worker representatives, consultation meetings), its procedural rules (mandatory consultation on safety changes, protected reporting without retaliation), and its persistence mechanism (institutionalized through labor regulations, collective agreements, and management systems that sustain worker voice in safety governance). A safety-feedback is a structured loop through which information about safety performance — incidents, near-misses, audit findings, observations, and metrics — is collected, analyzed, and communicated back to relevant stakeholders to inform decisions and drive continuous improvement. It is defined by its data sources (incident reports, safety observations, audit findings), its analysis methods (trend analysis, root-cause review, benchmarking), and its communication mechanisms (safety bulletins, team briefings, dashboards, one-on-one coaching). The feedback loop closes when recipients act on the information, producing observable changes in behavior or conditions that are themselves fed back as performance data. [formal: feedback safetyis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety-awareness is the structured cognitive recognition of hazards, risks, and unsafe conditions within an environment. Its parameters are: (1) scope — the specific domain (workplace, home, public space); (2) depth — from basic hazard identification to nuanced risk perception; (3) trigger modality — visual, auditory, procedural, or experiential cues. It persists through: repeated exposure to safety communications, reflective practice after near-misses and incidents, environmental cues like signage and markings, and organizational reinforcement through recognition of safe behavior. Unlike safety-training, which delivers structured knowledge, safety-awareness operates continuously as a state of situational vigilance — the background processing that makes hazard recognition automatic rather than deliberative. It is cultivated through a mix of awareness campaigns, visible safety infrastructure, peer modeling, and post-event reflection that recalibrates one's perception of risk. [formal: cognitio_periculi | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Coaching is a structured interpersonal method for developing individual capability through guided reflection, goal-setting, and performance feedback. The coach facilitates learning and change without delivering content directly, distinguishing coaching from teaching and mentoring. [formal: coaching | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Transparency is the institutional practice of making information accessible, visible, and disclosed to stakeholders. Its parameters are: (1) scope — what information is covered (records, data, decisions, processes); (2) audience — who receives it (public, regulators, employees, stakeholders); (3) mechanism — the means of disclosure (open-records laws, mandatory publication, active publication, audit trails); (4) enforcement — compliance structures (oversight bodies, penalties for concealment, whistleblower protections). The persistence mechanism is legal requirement combined with institutional norm and technological infrastructure (public databases, access portals). [formal: transparentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A leading indicator is a forward-looking measurement construct that tracks inputs, activities, or early conditions to predict and influence future outcomes. Its parameters are: (1) domain — the outcome area being predicted (safety, financial, operational, health); (2) signal — the specific activity or condition measured as the leading signal; (3) time-horizon — the interval between signal observation and outcome realization; (4) threshold — the value or range at which the signal triggers action. The persistence mechanism is analytical frameworks and management practice that define what counts as a signal and how it is measured over time. [formal: index praevius | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A key performance indicator (KPI) is a quantified measure used to evaluate the success of an organization or individual against strategic objectives. Its parameters are: (1) domain — the functional area being measured (financial, operational, customer, etc.); (2) threshold — the target value that defines success or failure; (3) frequency — how often the metric is calculated and reviewed; (4) owner — the role accountable for the indicator. KPIs persist through management reporting systems, dashboards, and performance review cycles that make strategy operational. [formal: kpi | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A trailing indicator is the most recent data point in a time-ordered sequence of measurements, used to signal the current state or short-term trajectory of a monitored phenomenon. Its parameters are: (1) domain — the measured variable (e.g., latency, throughput, error rate, inventory count); (2) window — the span of recent observations from which the trailing value is drawn (e.g., last reading, last N samples); (3) persistence — stored in logs, dashboards, and alerting systems that retain timestamped observation streams for ongoing comparison against thresholds or historical baselines. It extends human monitoring capacity by distilling a temporal sequence into a single readable value, making it possible to assess whether a process is stable, drifting, or deviating. [formal: indicium posterius | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

A safety-threshold is a defined boundary — quantitative or qualitative — that separates acceptable risk levels from unacceptable ones within a safety management system. It is established through risk assessment, regulatory requirement, or operational analysis, and persists via institutional documentation, standard operating procedures, and automated monitoring systems that trigger responses when breached. [formal: limen | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A risk-control is a deliberately designed measure or set of measures — policies, procedures, technical safeguards, or organizational practices — that reduces, transfers, or eliminates the probability or impact of a specified risk. Its parameters are: (1) the risk target (what is being controlled), (2) the control type (preventive, detective, corrective, or directive), (3) the implementation mechanism (technology, process, training, or governance), and (4) the residual risk level (the risk remaining after the control is applied). It persists through documented standards, repeatable implementation processes, and institutional review cycles that validate and update controls over time. [formal: control | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Preventive action is a structured safety practice that identifies, evaluates, and eliminates the root causes of potential nonconformities or hazards before they materialize into actual incidents. It operates prospectively rather than reactively: the procedure triggers when risk assessments, trend analyses, audit findings, or hazard reviews surface conditions that *could* cause harm, and prescribes targeted interventions to remove those conditions from the operational environment. Unlike corrective action, which addresses a nonconformity that has already occurred, preventive action targets the causal chain upstream. Its persistence mechanism is organizational: codified in safety management systems (e.g., ISO 45001 procedures), documented in standard operating protocols, and enforced through management review cycles that verify the action was taken and evaluate its effectiveness. The practice is explicit — it is written, taught, audited, and measured — and persists across organizational memory through documented procedures, training programs, and institutional routines that outlast individual practitioners. [formal: actio praeventiva | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Safety intervention is a structured set of deliberate actions deployed to reduce, control, or eliminate hazards and prevent incidents before they materialize. Its parameters are: (1) a identified hazard or risk scenario, (2) a chosen control measure drawn from a hierarchy of effectiveness (elimination, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, personal protective equipment), and (3) an implementation pathway through organizational procedures. It persists through written protocols, training programs, enforcement mechanisms, and periodic review cycles embedded in organizational practice. The intervention is distinguished from spontaneous reaction by its planned nature and from routine operations by its specific focus on hazard reduction. [formal: interventio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A poka-yoke is a mistake-proofing mechanism built into a process or device that prevents human errors from occurring or makes them immediately obvious so they can be corrected before causing defects. Originating in the Toyota Production System, poka-yokes rely on simple physical constraints, sensors, or procedural checks — such as a plug that only fits one orientation, a fixture that detects a missing part, or a checklist that blocks progression until all items are marked complete — rather than relying on human memory or vigilance. The mechanism persists through design specifications, manufacturing tooling, and standardized work instructions carried across the production lifecycle.
[formal: poka-yoke | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Error-prevention is the systematic practice of designing systems, processes, and environments to stop human errors, procedural failures, and organizational lapses from occurring. Its parameters include: (1) targeting error modes — slips, lapses, mistakes, and violations as classified by human factors research; (2) applying preventive controls — poka-yokes, standardization, redundancy, constraint design, and workload management; (3) operating before an incident — unlike error-detection which catches errors after they occur, error-prevention aims to eliminate the conditions that enable errors. It persists through safety management systems, regulatory frameworks, engineering standards, and institutional knowledge encoded in procedures and training curricula. [formal: preventio-errorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Scrum is a human-made framework for iterative project management and product development. Its parameters: (1) three defined roles — product owner (prioritizes work), scrum master (facilitates process and removes impediments), and development team (cross-functional deliverers); (2) time-boxed sprints typically 1–4 weeks; (3) four ceremonies — sprint planning, daily stand-up, sprint review, and sprint retrospective; (4) artifacts — product backlog, sprint backlog, and the increment. It persists through organizational practice, training programs, and the body of knowledge codified in the Scrum Guide. The framework is designed for empirical process control in complex product development where requirements evolve.

A safety-trainer is a human-made role defined by three operational parameters: (1) curriculum design — the creation of structured instructional content covering specific hazards, protocols, and competencies relevant to a defined work environment; (2) instructional delivery — the conduct of formal teaching sessions, whether classroom-based, on-site, or simulated, using pedagogical methods adapted to the audience; (3) competence assessment — the evaluation of trainee understanding and skill through tests, practical demonstrations, or observed performance. The construct persists through institutional practice (job descriptions, certification requirements, regulatory mandates) and through the training materials and records it produces. The safety-trainer is distinguished from general safety communication by the requirement of formal curriculum, scheduled delivery, and documented assessment outcomes. [formal: instructor safetyis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A bottleneck is a constraint — a resource, process step, capacity limit, or rule — that determines the maximum output rate of an entire system. It is identified by measuring flow through each stage and locating the one with the lowest throughput relative to demand. The concept persists through diagnostic methods (Theory of Constraints five focusing steps, constraint analysis), visual modeling (throughput maps, dependency diagrams), and institutional practice (operations management curricula, lean manufacturing, agile flow metrics). It is explicitly recognized and actively managed in industrial engineering and systems thinking. [formal: null | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Competency is a demonstrated ability — the proven combination of knowledge, skill, and judgment that enables effective, safe performance in a defined domain. It is assessed through observable performance against established standards and persists through documented evidence, periodic re-assessment, and the institutional memory of certification bodies. Assessment methods include direct observation, practical examination, and portfolio review. [formal: competentia | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An indicator is a human-made measurable observable that conveys information about the state, trend, or performance of some condition or system. Its parameters are: (1) a reference condition or system whose state it tracks; (2) a measurement method that maps raw observations to a signal; (3) a threshold or baseline against which the signal is evaluated. An indicator persists through measurement systems, data collection practices, and the conventions that assign meaning to particular signal values — it is not the thing measured, but the constructed lens through which the thing is rendered legible. [formal: indicium | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-moment is a brief, focused safety discussion delivered at the start of a meeting, shift, or gathering — typically 2-5 minutes long. Its parameters are: (1) a single safety topic or hazard drawn from the participants' actual work context; (2) a facilitator who presents the topic and leads a brief reflection; (3) a connection to the audience's own work or experience. A safety-moment persists through organizational safety culture, meeting agendas, and the practice of sharing safety observations peer-to-peer. It is distinct from formal safety-training in its brevity, informality, and topical immediacy. [formal: moment of safety | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A safety-symptom is an observable indicator that a safety failure or incident may be imminent. Its persistence mechanism: organizational safety reporting systems, near-miss databases, safety training curricula, and risk assessment protocols that codify what counts as a symptom and how to respond. Without these human-made structures, near-misses remain unclassified incidents rather than diagnostic safety-symptoms. [formal: signum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

[formal: propositum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A near-miss is an unplanned event that had the potential to cause harm, injury, or damage but did not, due to chance, luck, or timely intervention. A safety-walk is a structured observational practice in which a designated person moves systematically through work areas to observe conditions, engage workers in conversation about hazards and near-misses, and identify emerging risks before they manifest as incidents. Unlike checklist inspections, the safety-walk relies on conversational inquiry and situational awareness, making it effective at surfacing latent conditions that standard checklists miss. A safety-hierarchy-of-controls is a structured decision framework used in occupational safety to prioritize risk mitigation measures by their effectiveness. It ranks controls from most to least protective: elimination of the hazard, substitution with a less hazardous alternative, engineering controls that isolate people from the hazard, administrative controls that change work practices, and personal protective equipment that protects the worker. The hierarchy serves safety-management by providing a systematic approach to selecting interventions, with higher-order controls offering greater reliability and independence from human behavior. [formal: gradus | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A safety-walk is a structured observational practice in organizational safety management, where designated individuals systematically move through work areas to observe physical conditions, engage workers in conversation about hazards and near-misses, and identify risks proactively before incidents occur. Safety-snapshot is a point-in-time record of an organization's safety status, capturing key indicators, conditions, and compliance status at a specific moment. Safety-prevention is the organized set of practices, procedures, and institutional commitments designed to anticipate hazards, eliminate risk factors, and prevent occupational harm before it occurs. A safety-near-miss is the organizational categorization of events that possessed a causal pathway toward harm but did not result in actual damage, injury, or loss, because of chance circumstances or timely intervention. Its parameters: (1) an identifiable hazard or failure mode was present, (2) the chain toward harm was underway, (3) actual harm was averted by luck or intervention, and (4) the event is recorded or reported for organizational learning.
