[formal: diagramma sensitivitatis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cook's distance is a human-made statistical measure used in regression analysis to quantify the influence of each individual observation on the fitted regression coefficients. It carves a scalar value computed from the residual, leverage, and coefficient estimates of a regression model — specifically, the standardized change in the fitted values when observation i is deleted. Large Cook's distance values flag observations whose removal would materially alter the model, making it a tool for identifying influential data points that warrant closer inspection. The persistence mechanism is the mathematical formula itself, encoded in every major statistical software package (R, Python statsmodels, SAS, SPSS) and taught in regression courses as a standard diagnostic. [formal: distantia Cook | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diagnostic plot is a visual encoding designed to reveal structural properties of a dataset or model fit — outliers, leverage, influence, heteroscedasticity, model misspecification, and distributional assumptions. A sensitivity plot is a visual encoding that displays how a model's predictions or outputs change as one or more input parameters vary. It carves by method: the plot persists a systematic perturbation of inputs (one-at-a-time or in combination) and records the resulting output deltas. Its persistence mechanism is the plotting convention — typically a line or scatter plot with a parameter on one axis and a response metric on the other — maintained by sensitivity-analysis practice in computational modelling. [formal: sensitivus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The hat matrix H is the n×n projection matrix in ordinary least squares regression such that y-hat equals Hy, where y is the vector of observed responses and y-hat the vector of fitted values. H equals X(X-transpose X) inverse X-transpose for design matrix X. Its diagonal elements h-sub-i-i called leverages measure the influence of observation i on its own fitted value. The trace of H equals p the number of regression parameters including the intercept. The matrix is a human-made algebraic device that persists through the linear algebra formalism of regression theory. [formal: matrix praedium | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A scale-location plot is a diagnostic scatterplot used in regression analysis to assess whether the variance of residuals is constant across fitted values. It maps each fitted value on the x-axis to the square root of the absolute standardized residuals on the y-axis; a horizontal band indicates homoscedasticity, while a funnel or trend indicates heteroscedasticity. It carves by its axes (fitted values vs sqrt(|standardized residuals|)), its purpose (heteroscedasticity detection), and its persistence mechanism (graphical formalism embedded in statistical software). [formal: plot-sit | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diagnostic plot is a class of visualization used in statistical modeling to assess model adequacy by examining residuals, leverage, and influential observations. The graph persists as a formal model encoded in data structures (adjacency matrices, edge lists) and transmitted through scientific literature, software libraries (e.g., DoWhy, pgmpy, causalgraphicalmodels), and computational frameworks that perform causal discovery and inference. The structure enables querying counterfactuals, identifying confounders via d-separation, and computing do-calculus interventions.\n\n[formal: causal_graph | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An added-variable plot (also called a partial regression plot) is a regression diagnostic scatterplot that isolates the relationship between one predictor variable and the response by plotting the residuals of the response regressed on all other predictors against the residuals of that single predictor regressed on all other predictors. It allows inspection of linearity, outliers, and influential points for each covariate independently of the full model. The chart persists through statistical software implementations (R, Python, SAS), textbooks, and academic practice. [formal: en | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A variance inflation factor is a scalar measure computed for each predictor in a multiple regression model. For predictor X_j, let R²_j be the coefficient of determination when X_j is regressed on all other predictors. The VIF is VIF_j = 1 / (1 - R²_j). The persistence mechanism is mathematical definition applied to any fitted regression model. [formal: varietatis inflationis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A propensity score is the conditional probability of a unit receiving a treatment or exposure, given a set of observed covariates. It is computed by fitting a statistical model (typically logistic regression or a generalized linear model) to observed covariates and treatment assignment, then predicting the probability for each unit. Propensity scores are used to balance covariate distributions between treated and control groups, enabling causal inference from observational data via matching, stratification, weighting, or regression adjustment. [formal: propensity_score | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A partial regression plot (also called an added-variable plot) is a scatter plot that visualizes the marginal relationship between a single predictor and the response in a multiple regression model, after removing the linear effects of all other predictors. It is constructed by computing two residual quantities: (1) the residuals of the response variable regressed on all predictors except the one of interest, and (2) the residuals of that predictor regressed on all remaining predictors. Plotting the first against the second, the slope of the ordinary least squares line through the points equals the coefficient of that predictor in the full model. The plot reveals nonlinearity, heteroscedasticity, outliers, and the strength and direction of the adjusted relationship. [formal: grāfica residuōrum partialium | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Busywork is a human-made organizational practice consisting of activities that signal effort or compliance while producing negligible substantive value. Parameters: (1) the activity is observable and reportable — it leaves a trace that can be presented as evidence of work; (2) the activity's primary function is performative rather than instrumental; (3) participants (at least some) recognize the gap between appearance and substance. [formal: occupatio inutilis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A partial residual plot (also called a component-plus-residual plot) is a scatter plot used in multiple regression analysis to assess whether a predictor variable has a linear relationship with the response. It displays the partial residuals (observed response minus the contribution of all other predictors) against the predictor variable of interest, with a lowess or linear reference line to indicate the trend. Parameters: (1) one predictor variable is selected for display; (2) partial residuals are computed by adding the estimated coefficient of that predictor to the residual from the full model; (3) a reference line (flat or fitted) shows whether the relationship is linear or curved. Persistence mechanism: the plot persists through statistical software implementation and teaching in regression methodology, maintained as a standard diagnostic in applied statistics. [formal: partialis residualis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A studentized residual is a residual value from a regression model that has been standardized by an estimate of its standard deviation, enabling observation-level comparison and outlier detection. Parameters: (1) the raw residual is the difference between observed and predicted values; (2) the standard deviation is estimated from the data excluding the observation itself (externally studentized) or including it (internally studentized); (3) the resulting value follows approximately a t-distribution, allowing formal outlier testing. Persistence: the statistic is computed algorithmically from fitted regression models and persists as a computed value in statistical software outputs and published diagnostic tables. [formal: residuum studentizatum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Bootstrapping is a statistical resampling method that estimates the sampling distribution of a statistic (e.g. mean, median, regression coefficient) by repeatedly drawing samples with replacement from the observed dataset. Parameters: (1) B — the number of bootstrap replications (typically 1,000+), (2) the original dataset of n observations, (3) the statistic function to compute on each bootstrap sample. Persistence: implemented as a computational algorithm in statistical software (R, Python, SAS) and codified in statistical theory as a non-parametric inference technique. [formal: bootstrap | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A tolerance interval is a statistical construct for population-level uncertainty quantification. It specifies a range that, with a specified confidence level (1-alpha), contains at least a specified proportion (p) of the underlying population distribution. Parameters: (1) the confidence level — the probability that the interval covers the specified proportion, (2) the coverage proportion — the fraction of the population to be contained, (3) sample statistics (mean, standard deviation) used to compute the interval bounds. Persistence mechanism: mathematical formula applied to sample data to produce interval bounds that account for both sampling variability and population spread, documented in statistical practice and software implementations. [formal: interval tolerance | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A tolerance interval is a statistical construct for population-level uncertainty quantification. A standardized residual is a statistical transformation that divides each residual (the difference between an observed value and its fitted value) by an estimate of its standard deviation. This standardization produces values that are approximately standard normal under model assumptions, enabling cross-observation comparison and outlier detection. Parameters: (1) the raw residual r_i = y_i - ŷ_i, (2) the estimated standard deviation of that residual s(r_i) derived from the model's error structure, (3) the resulting standardized value z_i = r_i / s(r_i). Persistence mechanism: algebraic computation applied to regression residuals, standardized through division by estimated standard error. [formal: residual standardizatum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A dfbeta is a regression diagnostic measure that quantifies how much each individual regression coefficient changes when a single observation is deleted from the model. For observation i and coefficient j, it is computed as dfbeta_j(i) = (beta_j - beta_j(i)) / SE(beta_j(i)), where beta_j is the original coefficient and beta_j(i) is the coefficient estimated with observation i removed. The denominator standardizes the change so that coefficients on different scales can be compared. Values exceeding ±2 flag influential observations for each predictor. This construct persists through statistical software packages, regression analysis practice, and the methodological literature on regression diagnostics. [formal: df-beta | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A dfits measure is a regression diagnostic that quantifies the standardized difference between the fitted values from the full model and the fitted values from the model fit after deleting a single observation. For observation i, dfits_i = (y_hat_i - y_hat_i^(i)) / (s_i^(i) * sqrt(h_ii)), where y_hat_i is the fitted value, y_hat_i^(i) is the leave-one-out fitted value, s_i^(i) is the delete-i standard error estimate, and h_ii is the leverage of observation i from the hat matrix. It is computed algorithmically from regression output and persists through statistical software implementations and published diagnostic tables. [formal: dfits | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A partial leverage plot (also known as a component leverage plot) is a regression diagnostic visualization that decomposes the overall leverage of each observation into contributions from individual predictors. Each data point is assigned a partial leverage value for each predictor variable, allowing analysts to see which specific variables drive a point's influence on the regression model.

The plot is constructed by computing the component leverage h_i(j) = (x_i(j) - x̄(j))² / Σ_k(x_k(j) - x̄(j))² for each observation i and predictor j, then displaying these values graphically — typically as a bar chart or scatter plot ordered by observation. Partial leverage plots are produced by standard statistical software packages (R's car package, Python's statsmodels) and are used in diagnostic regression analysis to pinpoint which predictor(s) cause a given observation to exert disproportionate influence.

[formal: partial_leverage_plot | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A regression diagnostic is a class of statistical methods used to evaluate whether a fitted regression model satisfies its underlying assumptions and to identify observations that disproportionately affect the model's parameter estimates or predictions. It comprises residual analysis tools (residual plots, Cook's distance, DFFITS, DFBETAS), influence measures, and assumption checks (linearity, homoscedasticity, normality of errors, independence). The framework persists through statistical textbooks, software documentation (R, Python statsmodels, SAS), and standard practice in empirical research workflows. [formal: diagnosticus regressionis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

A regression diagnostic is a class of statistical methods used to evaluate whether a fitted regression model satisfies its underlying assumptions and to identify observations that disproportionately affect parameter estimates or predictions. It comprises techniques including residual analysis, influence measures (Cook's distance, DFBETA, DFFITS), leverage assessment, and diagnostic plots (residual-vs-fitted, normal Q-Q, scale-location, partial residual). [formal: diagnosys regressionis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Normalized residuals are regression diagnostics obtained by dividing each raw residual r_i by the square root of MSE times (1 - h_ii), where h_ii is the i-th diagonal element of the hat matrix and MSE is the mean squared error of the fitted model. Unlike raw residuals, normalized residuals have approximately unit variance under the regression assumptions, making them suitable for identifying outliers across observations with differing leverage values. Values with absolute magnitude exceeding 2 are typically flagged as outliers. [formal: normalized-residual | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cook's distance is a regression diagnostic measure that quantifies the influence of each observation on the fitted regression coefficients. It is computed as D_i = (r_i^2 / (p * MSE)) * (h_ii / (1 - h_ii)^2) where r_i is the i-th standardized residual, h_ii is the i-th diagonal element of the hat matrix, p is the number of regression parameters, and MSE is the mean squared error. Large values of D_i indicate observations that, if removed, would substantially change the fitted model. It persists through statistical practice and software implementation. [formal: cook_distantia | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An influential observation is a data point in a regression dataset whose removal would meaningfully alter the fitted model's coefficients or predictions. It is identified through diagnostic measures — Cook's distance, DFBETAS, dfits, and leverage — that quantify each observation's outsized impact on estimation. The concept persists through statistical software implementations, diagnostic procedures, and methodological literature that operationalize its detection and handling. [formal: observatio influens | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A diagnostic measure is a numerical statistic computed from a fitted statistical model and its data to evaluate model adequacy, flag problematic observations, or check assumption violations. Each measure isolates a specific aspect of model behavior — influence on coefficients (Cook's distance, DFBETAS), sensitivity of fitted values (dfits), predictor-space extremity (leverage), or unexplained variation (residuals). The concept persists through statistical software implementations, methodological standards, and diagnostic reporting protocols. [formal: mensura diagnostica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A normal probability plot is a diagnostic visualization that maps the ordered residuals of a statistical model to the theoretical quantiles of a standard normal distribution, producing a Q-Q plot where systematic deviations from the reference line indicate departures from normality in the error structure. The plot is constructed by sorting residuals in ascending order, computing empirical cumulative probabilities via rank-based formulas, converting these to z-scores through the inverse normal cumulative distribution function, and displaying the pairs on a scatter plot with the reference line y=x. It persists as a standardized diagnostic output in statistical software packages and as a taught method in regression analysis curricula. [formal: normal_probability_plot | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dfbetas is a regression diagnostic measure that computes the standardized change in each regression coefficient β_i resulting from the deletion of a single observation j from the fitting data. For a model with p predictors and n observations, dfbetas_ij = (β_i - β_i^(−j)) / se(β_i), where β_i^(−j) is the coefficient estimated without observation j and se(β_i) is the standard error of the coefficient. The measure is computed by statistical software packages (R, Python statsmodels, SAS) and reported in regression diagnostic output. It persists through the conventions of statistical computing practice and diagnostic reporting protocols. [formal: df_betas | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A hat matrix is a human-made mathematical construct in linear regression analysis that maps observed response values to fitted values. It is an n×n projection matrix H = X(X'X)^{-1}X' where X is the design matrix, and its diagonal elements h_ii (leverage values) quantify how much each observation influences its own fitted value. The matrix persists through algebraic computation in statistical software and textbooks. [formal: matrix | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A studentized residual is a human-made statistical measure used in regression analysis to identify outliers. It adjusts raw residuals by dividing by an estimate of their standard deviation, accounting for the fact that residuals have non-constant variance. There are two types: internally studentized (using a pooled variance estimate) and externally studentized (using a variance estimate computed without the observation in question). It persists through statistical software implementations and textbooks. [formal: measure | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A leverage residual is a human-made diagnostic construct in linear regression analysis that combines residual magnitude with observation leverage to flag influential data points. It is computed as r_i * sqrt((1 - h_ii) / h_ii) where r_i is the raw residual for observation i and h_ii is the i-th diagonal element of the hat matrix H = X(X'X)^{-1}X'. The construct persists as a standard computed quantity in statistical software output (R, Python statsmodels, SAS) and in published regression diagnostic tables. [formal: residual_analysis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Regression analysis is a human-made statistical methodology for estimating the functional relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. Press residual (also called the studentized deleted residual or leave-one-out residual) is a diagnostic measure in regression analysis that quantifies the discrepancy between an observation's actual value and the value predicted by a model fit to all other observations. The statistic ranges from 0 to 4: values near 2 indicate no autocorrelation, values below 2 suggest positive autocorrelation, and values above 2 suggest negative autocorrelation. The test compares d against critical values from the Durbin-Watson distribution, which depend on sample size, number of predictors, and significance level. Persistence mechanism: the test endures as a standardized diagnostic routine embedded in statistical software packages (R, Python statsmodels, SAS, Stata), transmitted through econometrics and applied regression textbooks, and applied as a standard step in regression assumption validation workflows. A significance level (α) is set in advance as the rejection threshold. The procedure persists through the scientific method, statistical education, and regulatory decision-making. The parameters that define a statistical test include the hypothesis structure, the chosen test statistic, the underlying sampling distribution assumptions, the significance threshold, and whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed. A statistical test persists through formal documentation in statistical textbooks, implementation in statistical software packages (R, Python's scipy, SAS), and sustained academic and industry practice. The concept enables identification of repeating patterns, trend detection, and model diagnostics — a non-zero autocorrelation in regression residuals signals misspecification (e.g. omitted variables or wrong functional form). Its persistence mechanism is computation from data and communication through statistical practice, formalized in the correlogram and partial autocorrelation function. This quantity determines the shape of sampling distributions (t, chi-squared, F) used for inference and controls the trade-off between model complexity and estimation reliability. Cross-validation is a statistical procedure for estimating how well a predictive model generalizes to unseen data. It partitions a dataset into k subsets (folds), iteratively trains the model on k-1 folds and validates on the remaining fold, then aggregates the validation scores. Parameters: k (number of folds, typically 5 or 10), the partitioning scheme (random, grouped, or ordered), and the aggregation method (mean, median). The method persists through implementation in software libraries (scikit-learn, R), standardized protocols in machine learning competitions, and textbooks on statistical learning. [formal: cross-validatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Graph theory is a mathematical framework for studying structures composed of nodes (vertices) connected by edges (links). It provides formal definitions for graph types (directed, undirected, weighted, bipartite), operations (traversal, embedding, decomposition), and properties (connectivity, planarity, chromatic number). Parameters: vertex sets, edge sets, and optional weights or labels. Persistence mechanism: abstract mathematical formalism encoded in set theory and implemented through computational algorithms that model networks across computer science, social sciences, and logistics.

A hypothesis test is a statistical procedure for making decisions about population parameters based on sample data. It formalizes the process of evaluating evidence by specifying a null hypothesis (default assumption), an alternative hypothesis, a test statistic, and a significance level (alpha) that controls the probability of Type I error. Parameters: null and alternative hypotheses, test statistic, significance level, and sample data. Persistence mechanism: mathematical formalism in probability theory, operationalized through standardized procedures (t-test, chi-squared test, ANOVA) that provide decision rules for accepting or rejecting the null hypothesis based on whether the observed test statistic falls in the rejection region.

Data cleaning is a quality assurance practice that identifies, corrects, or removes errors, inconsistencies, and irrelevant data from datasets to improve data quality for analysis. It encompasses operations including handling missing values (imputation, deletion), detecting and correcting outliers, resolving duplicates, standardizing formats, and validating constraints (range checks, type checks, referential integrity). Parameters: the dataset, the quality rules and constraints, and the cleaning procedures applied. Persistence mechanism: procedural methodology encoded in data management protocols and implemented through systematic workflows (validation rules, transformation scripts, quality metrics) that maintain data integrity across its lifecycle.

A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic (e.g. mean, variance, proportion) computed over all possible samples of a fixed size drawn from a population. It is parameterized by (1) the underlying population distribution, (2) the statistic being computed, and (3) the sample size. It persists through mathematical formalization (measure theory on sample spaces), computational simulation (Monte Carlo estimation), and pedagogical practice (central to statistical inference). The sampling distribution is not the population itself nor the observed data — it is a theoretical construct that describes how a statistic varies across hypothetical repetitions of the sampling process. [formal: distributio samplingis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Few-shot learning is a machine learning paradigm where a model acquires the ability to perform a new task from K exemplars (typically K ∈ {1, 5, 10, 32}), by transferring structural knowledge acquired from a distribution of related source tasks. Parameters: K = support set size, N = number of classes in the support set, query set size Q, task distribution p(T) over source tasks, and the embedding function h_θ that maps inputs to a representation space where similarity-based classification generalizes to novel tasks. Measurement error is the human-made statistical construct that quantifies the difference between an observed measurement and the true value of the quantity being measured. The construct persists through calibration protocols, uncertainty budgets, and the formal language of error analysis used in metrology and experimental science. Measurement error is categorized into systematic error (bias affecting all measurements consistently) and random error (stochastic variation across repeated measurements), each with distinct correction strategies and propagation rules used in scientific inference and quality assurance.\n\n[formal: error_metria | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Sampling distribution is the human-made probability-theoretic construct that describes the probability distribution of a statistic (such as a mean, variance, or proportion) computed across all possible samples of a given size drawn from a population. The construct persists through the theoretical framework of inferential statistics, where it serves as the foundation for confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, and standard error calculations. A sampling distribution is distinguished from the population distribution (which describes individual observations) and the empirical distribution of a single sample (which describes observed values). The Central Limit Theorem provides the key approximation: for sufficiently large n, the sampling distribution of the mean converges to a normal distribution regardless of the population shape.\n\n[formal: distributio_sampling | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Self-supervised learning is a machine learning paradigm where models extract supervision from unlabeled data by generating pseudo-labels from the data's own structure. Computational complexity is a theoretical framework that classifies computational problems by the resources — primarily time and space — required to solve them, regardless of any specific algorithm or machine implementation. The persistence mechanism is the formal mathematical theory encoded in textbooks, proofs, and peer-reviewed literature. [formal: complexitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

Significance level (alpha) is a human-made threshold in statistical hypothesis testing — the maximum acceptable probability of a Type I error (rejecting a true null hypothesis). Standard values are 0.05 and 0.01, chosen by convention to balance error rates against the power of a test. It operationalizes the trade-off between false positives and false negatives in decision-making under uncertainty. The persistence mechanism is the statistical convention encoded in textbooks, software documentation, and scientific reporting standards. [formal: gradus significantis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.90]

A prediction interval is a statistical procedure that, given a sample and a future observation (or set of observations), produces a range that is expected to contain the future value with a specified confidence level. Unlike a confidence interval for a population parameter, a prediction interval accounts for both the uncertainty in the estimated parameters and the inherent variability of the individual observation. It is computed from the sampling distribution of the prediction error, combining the standard error of the mean estimate with the residual standard deviation. [formal: intervallo predictionis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A sampling distribution is the probability distribution of a statistic (such as the mean, variance, or proportion) obtained by repeatedly drawing random samples of a fixed size from a population. It describes how the value of the statistic varies across all possible samples of that size. The sampling distribution of the sample mean, for example, is centered at the population mean and has standard error equal to the population standard deviation divided by the square root of the sample size. Sampling distributions form the theoretical foundation for confidence intervals, hypothesis testing, and prediction intervals. [formal: distributio sampling | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Curriculum learning is a training strategy in machine learning in which examples are presented to the model in a specific order—typically progressing from easy to difficult—so that the learner develops robust internal representations before tackling harder cases. Working-memory-capacity is the quantified extent of working memory, measured as the upper bound on simultaneous information storage and manipulation that a given individual can sustain across trials. It is constructed through psychometric operationalization: span tasks (reading span, operation span, simple span) count items correctly retained amid concurrent processing; change-detection measures K (the number of visual objects retained); n-back tracks accuracy at graded memory loads. The resulting score is treated as a latent trait variable with test-retest stability and predictive validity for complex cognitive performance (fluid reasoning, reading comprehension, dual-task coordination). Parameters: the construct assumes (1) a bounded capacity rather than an unbounded buffer, (2) a single scalar summary of individual differences, (3) operationalization through standardized tasks whose validity is established by convergent correlation with external criteria. Persistence mechanism: the measure persists through repeated administration across populations, calibration against cognitive models (Cowan's K, Oberauer's restricted-activation model), and replication in the cognitive psychology literature. [formal: capax memoriae activae | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

The mechanism of persistence is the concept itself — encoded in cognitive-psychology literature, educational theory, and skill-acquisition research across decades. A predictive model is a human-constructed artifact that maps input features to predicted outcomes, calibrated through training on labeled or unlabeled historical data. Deep learning is a subclass of machine learning defined by neural networks with three or more layers, where each layer learns a progressively higher-level abstraction of the data. [formal: doctrina profunda | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Automaticity is the cognitive process by which repeated, deliberate practice transforms effortful actions into fast, unconscious operations that execute without conscious attention or working-memory load. Its parameters are: (1) acquisition through repetition, (2) independence from conscious control, (3) reduced working-memory demand, and (4) resistance to interference once established. It persists through procedural memory consolidation — the neurocognitive shift from declarative to procedural knowledge — as skills become embedded in basal-ganglia circuits. A competent speaker would say automaticity is 'the transition from thinking about doing to doing without thinking.' [formal: automatizatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Memory consolidation is the neurocognitive process by which fragile, recently formed memories are stabilized into long-term storage through systems-level reorganization. Its parameters are: (1) a labile initial phase (minutes to hours) vulnerable to disruption, (2) synaptic consolidation via long-term potentiation at the circuit level, and (3) systems consolidation through hippocampal-neocortical replay during sleep. It persists as structural changes in cortical networks gradually assume responsibility for memory retrieval, reducing hippocampal dependence over time. The mechanism is experience-dependent neural plasticity, driven by replay and integrated into existing knowledge structures. [formal: consolidatio memoriae | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Episodic memory is the human-constructed category for a type of long-term memory that stores personally experienced events embedded with temporal and spatial context — the ability to re-experience a specific past episode as one's own. The process unfolds across stages: cognitive (understanding what to do), associative (refining how to do it), and autonomous (performing without conscious oversight). Zero-shot learning is a machine learning paradigm in which a trained model is evaluated on classes it never encountered during training. Instead of relying on labeled examples of target classes, the model bridges the training-test gap through auxiliary semantic information—such as attribute descriptions, word embeddings, or ontological relationships—that maps known classes to unknown ones in a shared semantic space. The mechanism of persistence is the structured semantic representation itself: once a vocabulary of attributes or embeddings exists, it can be reused across arbitrary zero-shot transfers without retraining. The approach emerged as deep learning models gained access to rich pre-trained embeddings (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe), enabling semantic generalization beyond visual features. Persistence: encoded as trainable parameters in software frameworks and serialized as model weights; the mathematical formalism persists in published literature and open-source implementations. The parameters defining an embedding are: (1) the vocabulary or item set being mapped, (2) the dimensionality of the vector space (typically 50–5000 dimensions), (3) the training objective or loss function that shapes the space (e.g., predicting co-occurrence, minimizing reconstruction error, or ranking based relevance), and (4) the optimization procedure (e.g., stochastic gradient descent) that adjusts vector values. The persistence mechanism is the learned weight matrix stored as model parameters in neural network architectures, persisted as serialized tensors in model files. The representation endures across sessions and deployments as long as the model weights are preserved.\n\n[formal: repraesentatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

user experience (UX) is the structured concept of how a human interacts with a system — the mental model, emotional response, and behavioral feedback loop formed through use. transformer is a class of neural network architecture built around self-attention mechanisms — a design where every position in a sequence can attend to every other position, enabling parallel processing of sequential data and capturing long-range dependencies. It is structured from stacked layers of multi-head attention and feed-forward sub-layers, connected by residual connections and layer normalization, with parameters updated via gradient-based optimization during training. The architecture persists as a parameterized computational graph whose weights encode learned representations. [formal: transformer | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

self-attention is a neural network mechanism where every position in a sequence computes attention weights over every other position in that same sequence — producing a context-aware representation for each position that depends on the full input. It carves by three parameters: (1) the query-key-value projection scheme that computes similarity scores between positions, (2) the normalization of those scores into a probability distribution over positions, and (3) the weighted aggregation of value vectors. The persistence mechanism is the algorithmic specification encoded in research papers, library implementations (e.g., PyTorch nn.MultiheadAttention), and the trained weights of deployed models. [formal: attentio se ipsa | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A search-engine is a computational system designed to locate, retrieve, and rank relevant items from a collection of data in response to a user query. Its operation rests on three parameters: (1) an index — an inverted mapping from searchable terms to the documents or records that contain them, enabling sub-linear lookup; (2) a query parser that transforms natural-language or structured input into indexable terms and operators; and (3) a ranking function that scores indexed items against the query and orders them by predicted relevance. A finite token buffer that defines the maximum span of text a language model can process in a single inference step. Semantic memory is the human-made cognitive category for storing general knowledge, facts, concepts, and meanings independent of personal experience or episodic recall. Episodic memory is the cognitive psychology construct for classifying a memory system that encodes and retrieves personal experiences — events tied to specific times, places, and emotional contexts. A feed-forward network (FFN) is a neural network module consisting of two linear projections separated by a non-linear activation function (ReLU or GELU). Given an input vector x and hidden dimension d_hidden, it computes FFN(x) = W2·activation(W1·x + b1) + b2. It is applied independently and identically to each position in a sequence. In transformer architectures, it follows the self-attention layer and provides the non-linear feature transformation that enables the model to learn complex representations beyond what linear attention alone can express. Its parameters are: input dimension d_model, hidden dimension d_hidden (typically 4×d_model), and the activation function. It persists through training as learnable weights and is deployed in every transformer-based model.\n\n[formal: feed-forward network | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A positional encoding is a human-designed method of injecting sequential position information into model representations, enabling architectures without inherent sequential bias (such as self-attention) to distinguish the relative or absolute position of elements in a sequence. It maps each position index to a vector — typically via fixed sinusoidal functions (sine and cosine at different frequencies) or learned embeddings — and adds or concatenates this vector to the token embeddings, producing position-aware representations that the model can attend to. The encoding persists as a designed pattern in neural network architecture: it is implemented in software, documented in papers and codebases, and replicated across transformer-based systems. Without positional encoding, attention mechanisms treat sequences as unordered sets, losing the temporal and structural information essential to language, time series, and ordered data.

[formal: positio artificialis | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Retrieval is the cognitive mechanism by which stored information is accessed and brought into active conscious processing. Parameters: (1) target — a previously encoded and stored memory trace; (2) cue — internal or external stimulus that triggers the search; (3) output — the recovered information, which may be complete, partial, or distorted. Persistence mechanism: cognitive science research, pedagogical practice, and linguistic convention maintain retrieval as a distinct concept from encoding, storage, and recall. Retrieval differs from mere recollection in that it includes both intentional and involuntary access, and from recognition in that it requires production rather than identification. The study of retrieval — including retrieval practice, retrieval-induced forgetting, and cue-dependent forgetting — establishes it as one of the three core processes of the memory system alongside encoding and storage. [formal: retriementum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Hallucination is a failure mode in generative AI systems where the model produces outputs that are factually incorrect, internally inconsistent, or ungrounded in the provided context, while presenting them with the same confidence as correct outputs. Parameters: (1) source — the grounding signal the model should have followed (training data, context window, retrieved documents); (2) manifestation — fabrication of details, conflation of distinct facts, or invention of non-existent entities/references; (3) detection — the gap between output plausibility and ground-truth verification. Persistence mechanism: the concept persists as a diagnostic category in ML safety literature, benchmarking protocols, and model evaluation practices. [formal: hallucinatio | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Weight-sharing is the architectural pattern wherein a single set of parameters is applied across multiple locations, layers, or time steps of a computational model. The concept persists through documentation in neural network literature, implementation in model architectures, and pedagogical transmission in machine learning curricula. [formal: participatio | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The key-value cache is a buffer that stores precomputed key and value tensors from transformer attention layers during autoregressive text generation. [formal: memoria chaverum | substrate: matter | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Parameters: candidate set size (k), scoring model type (cross-encoder, learning-to-rank, rule-based), retraining cycle.
