[formal: analysis-statistica | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mfcc (mel-frequency cepstral coefficients) is the human-made feature extraction technique that converts audio signals into a compact set of coefficients representing the short-term power spectrum envelope. Procedure: (1) frame the signal into overlapping windows; (2) compute the power spectrum via FFT; (3) pass the spectrum through a triangular Mel-scale filterbank; (4) take the log of each filterbank energy; (5) apply the discrete cosine transform. The resulting coefficients capture perceptually-relevant spectral shape and are the standard input for speech recognition and audio classification systems. Parameters: frame length (10–30 ms), number of filterbanks (typically 20–40), number of coefficients retained (typically 12–13). Persistence mechanism: standardized algorithm implemented in speech-processing software libraries and hardware codecs. [formal: mfcc | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral-domain is the human-made mathematical representation space in which cepstral coefficients are defined and manipulated. Constructed by: (1) computing the power spectrum of a signal via FFT; (2) taking the natural log of each frequency bin's magnitude; (3) applying the inverse Fourier transform. The resulting domain — parameterized by 'quefrency' (time-like variable in the cepstral domain) — is where cepstral analysis operates. Cepstral coefficients are samples in this domain. Unlike the time domain (original signal) or frequency domain (FFT output), the cepstral domain highlights periodic structures in the spectrum, making it ideal for pitch detection and spectral envelope analysis. Parameters: signal length, FFT size, windowing function. Persistence mechanism: mathematical construct implemented in signal-processing libraries. [formal: cepstral-domain | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mel-scale is the human-made perceptual frequency scale used in audio and speech processing. It maps linear Hertz frequencies to a scale where equal distances sound equally distant to human listeners. Construction: m = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700), where f is frequency in Hz and m is the value in mels. The scale was derived from Stevens, Volkmann, and Newman's (1937) psychoacoustic experiments and persists as a standardized mapping in audio processing software, speech recognition systems, and music information retrieval standards. [formal: mel | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mel-filterbank is a human-made array of triangular filterbanks spaced according to the mel frequency scale. Each filter overlaps its neighbors and spans a band of mel-spaced frequencies, collectively covering a target frequency range. The filterbank is applied to a spectral representation (typically a power spectrum) to produce a compressed set of energy values — one per filter — that approximates human auditory perception. Construction: for each frequency bin f in the spectrum, compute its mel value m(f) = 2595 * log10(1 + f/700), determine which two mel-scale points bracket m(f), and distribute the bin's energy proportionally. Used in MFCC pipelines and speech recognition systems. [formal: mel-filter-bank | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.94]

Harmonic is the human-made concept designating a tone whose frequency is an exact integer multiple of a fundamental frequency (n×f₀, n∈ℕ⁺). The concept carves a discrete set of frequency relationships that define timbre in acoustics, govern instrument resonance, structure tuning systems, and enable spectral decomposition in signal processing. It persists through mathematical notation (the harmonic series), musical notation, acoustic measurement, and teaching across physics and music theory. [formal: harmonicus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Speech-recognition is the human-made methodology and system for converting spoken language into text or structured representations through signal processing, linguistic modeling, and pattern classification. The concept carves a pipeline: audio capture → feature extraction (e.g. MFCC) → acoustic modeling → language modeling → decoding → text output. Persistence: implemented in software systems, standardized through benchmarks (e.g. Switchboard, LibriSpeech), and sustained by continuous research in deep learning and neural architectures. [formal: recognitio-verbalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral-liftering is a signal processing technique that applies a window-like function in the cepstral domain to selectively smooth or accentuate cepstral coefficients. It operates by applying a lifter (a low-pass, high-pass, or band-pass filter) to the cepstral coefficients before transforming back to the frequency domain. The parameters are: (1) the lifter type (low-pass for smoothing, high-pass for accentuating high-quefrency detail, band-pass for a specific quefrency band), (2) the cutoff quefrency, and (3) the order of the cepstral coefficients retained. The persistence mechanism is mathematical: the procedure is encoded in DSP algorithms and persists through software implementations in speech processing toolkits (HTK, Kaldi), research codebases, and textbook algorithms. The technique enables spectral envelope smoothing in MFCC extraction, voice conversion, and speech synthesis.\n\n[formal: lifter | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Zero-crossing-rate (ZCR) is the count or normalized rate of sign changes in a discrete-time audio signal within a defined analysis window. The parameters are: (1) the window size (typically 20-40ms for speech), (2) the window function applied before counting (usually Hamming or Hanning), (3) whether sign changes at exactly zero are counted (implementation detail that affects edge cases), and (4) normalization method (raw count vs. count per second). The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: ZCR is implemented as a standard computation in audio processing libraries and persists through code in librosa, LibROSA, MATLAB, Praat, and research codebases. It is a foundational feature for audio classification, speech voicing detection, onset detection, and timbre analysis.\n\n[formal: zcr | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-flatness is a signal processing feature that quantifies how sinusoidal (tonal) versus noise-like a power spectrum is. It is computed as the ratio of the geometric mean to the arithmetic mean of the spectral power values across frequency bins. Parameters: (1) the spectral estimate (periodogram, Welch's method, or spectrogram slice), (2) the frequency bands over which the mean is computed. A value near 1 indicates a flat (noise-like) spectrum; near 0 indicates a tonal (peaked) spectrum. It persists as a mathematical function implemented in DSP libraries and audio analysis software.\n\n[formal: planimetria | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Homomorphic filtering is a signal processing technique that decomposes a signal into convolutional or multiplicative components by mapping it into a domain where these operations become additive. The method applies three steps: (1) take the logarithm of the signal converting multiplication to addition and convolution to addition via the convolution theorem, (2) apply a linear filter in the transformed domain, (3) take the exponential to return to the original domain. The technique enables separation of source and channel effects for example in speech processing it separates vocal excitation from vocal tract filtering, and in image processing it separates illumination from reflectance. The mathematical foundation rests on the homomorphism property of the logarithm: log(a times b) equals log(a) plus log(b). The technique persists through its presence in standard DSP textbooks, implementation in libraries, and continued application in speech analysis, image restoration, and radar. [formal: filtrum homomorphum | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.67]

Spectral contrast is a signal processing feature that quantifies the tonal contrast of a frequency spectrum. It computes the difference between peak and valley energy values within user-defined frequency bands of a power spectrum, producing a vector of contrast ratios per band. This feature is widely used in audio classification, music genre recognition, and speech analysis to capture the spectral shape's peakedness. The technique was formalized by Jansen et al. (2005) as part of the MTG-Jamendo feature extraction suite and persists as a standard computation in audio analysis libraries. [formal: contrastus spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.75]

Spectral flux is a signal processing feature that quantifies the rate of change of the power spectrum over time. It operates by computing the power spectral density within successive overlapping windows and measuring the L1 distance (sum of absolute differences) between consecutive spectra. Parameters: (1) window size determines spectral resolution vs. temporal resolution trade-off; (2) hop size controls temporal granularity; (3) the spectral magnitude representation (linear, dB, Mel-scale) shapes sensitivity. Persistence mechanism: encoded in audio analysis pipelines across speech recognition (phoneme boundary detection), music information retrieval (onset detection, beat tracking), and acoustic event classification — standard in librosa, Essentia, and Praat.
[formal: fluxus spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral subtraction is a speech enhancement technique that reduces additive noise by operating in the cepstral domain. Introduced by Boll (1979), it works by computing the cepstrum of a noisy speech frame, identifying the quefrency range where noise dominates (typically low quefrency), estimating the noise cepstrum from silent/voiceless segments, and subtracting the noise cepstrum from the noisy cepstrum before inverse transformation. Parameters: (1) quefrency cutoff separates speech and noise components; (2) noise estimation strategy (initial segments, minimum statistics); (3) windowing parameters for spectral computation. Persistence mechanism: documented in the speech processing literature and implemented in toolkits like Praat and custom MATLAB/Python pipelines for noise robustness in ASR systems.
[formal: subtrahium cephstrale | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral rolloff is an audio signal processing feature that computes the frequency below which a specified percentage (commonly 85%) of the total spectral energy is concentrated. It operates by accumulating spectral magnitude values in descending frequency order until the energy threshold is met, then reporting the cutoff frequency bin. The feature captures spectral skew — whether energy is concentrated in lower or higher frequencies — and is a standard descriptor in timbre analysis, music information retrieval, and audio segmentation. [formal: rolloff_spectrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral bandwidth is the weighted standard deviation of frequency bins around the spectral centroid, computed from the power spectrum of a signal. Its parameters are: (1) the power spectrum P(k) giving magnitude at each frequency bin k, (2) the spectral centroid νc = Σk·P(k)/ΣP(k) as the weighting center, and (3) the bandwidth B = sqrt(ΣP(k)·(k − νc)² / ΣP(k)) as the spread measure. The persistence mechanism is mathematical computation applied frame-by-frame to the FFT-derived power spectrum, yielding a scalar value in frequency units (Hz) that quantifies how concentrated versus dispersed spectral energy is. Narrow bandwidth indicates energy clustered near the centroid (e.g., a pure tone); broad bandwidth indicates energy spread across the spectrum (e.g., noise). Used in audio classification, timbre analysis, and music information retrieval. [formal: latitudo spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Mel spectrum is the spectral representation of a signal obtained by applying a mel-scale triangular filterbank to its power spectrum. Its parameters are: (1) the input power spectrum P(f) giving energy at each linear frequency bin, (2) the mel filterbank matrix H(m,f) mapping linear frequency bins to mel frequency channels, and (3) the number of mel channels determining frequency resolution. Computation: M(m) = sum_f H(m,f) · P(f), yielding energy in each mel-frequency channel. Persistence: stored as a fixed-length vector of mel-channel energies, computable from any power spectrum via a deterministic filterbank application. [formal: spectrum melodicum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral representation is a mathematical encoding of a signal's frequency-domain structure. Its parameters are: (1) the input signal s(t) in the time domain, (2) the transform kernel K(f,t) that maps time to frequency (e.g., complex exponential for Fourier transform), (3) the resulting spectral function S(f) giving magnitude and phase at each frequency bin. The persistence mechanism is the computational procedure itself — the representation is stored as numerical arrays of frequency-magnitude pairs, and is reproducible from the original signal via the same transform. [formal: repraesentatio spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-energy is the total power or energy of a signal computed by integrating its power spectral density across all frequency components within a given analysis window. It is quantified as the sum of squared amplitude values across the spectrum, providing a scalar measure of a signal's overall intensity at each time frame. The concept persists through mathematical computation, audio analysis software, and scientific measurement frameworks. [formal: energia spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Power spectral density (PSD) is a spectral representation that quantifies the distribution of signal power across frequency. Computed via the Fourier transform of the autocorrelation function (Wiener–Khinchin theorem) or estimated from finite data using periodogram, Welch, or parametric methods, PSD maps how signal energy is allocated among frequency components. It enables characterization of dominant frequencies, bandwidth allocation, and noise spectral content. [formal: ps | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mel-filter-bank is a set of triangular overlapping filters spaced according to the mel scale, applied to a power spectrum or spectral representation to extract energy in perceptually-relevant frequency bands. Parameters: number of filters (typically 20-40), sample rate, and FFT window size. Persistence: computational — implemented as a fixed transformation matrix in audio and speech analysis software. [formal: mel-filter-bank | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A periodogram is a spectral estimation technique that computes the squared magnitude of the discrete Fourier transform of a signal to estimate its power spectral density. It converts a time-domain signal into a frequency-domain representation showing how the signal's power is distributed across frequencies. The method was introduced by Sir Harold Hotelling in 1935 as a direct, non-parametric approach to spectral analysis. It operates by taking the DFT of the signal, computing |DFT|^2 for each frequency bin, and normalizing by the signal length. The periodogram is the foundational method of spectral analysis, upon which smoothed and averaged variants (Welch's method, Bartlett's method) were developed to reduce variance. [formal: periodogram | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.10]

A bartlett method is a spectral estimation technique that computes a smoothed power spectrum estimate by partitioning a finite-length discrete signal into M non-overlapping segments of equal length L, computing the periodogram for each segment via magnitude-squared DFT, and averaging the M periodograms. The technique trades frequency resolution for variance reduction: the smoothing window is rectangular (width L), and the effective degrees of freedom scale linearly with the number of segments M. The method persists as a taught algorithm in digital signal processing curricula and as a standard routine in scientific computing libraries (NumPy, MATLAB). [formal: bartlett-method | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A nyquist-frequency is the theoretical upper bound on signal frequency that can be unambiguously represented after sampling at a given rate, defined as exactly half the sampling rate (fs/2). Frequencies above this bound fold back into the representable range, producing aliasing artifacts. The concept is defined by the Shannon-Nyquist sampling theorem and persists through mathematical formalism in information theory and digital signal processing. [formal: Nyquist | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A spectral-estimation technique infers the frequency-domain structure (power spectral density or amplitude distribution across frequencies) of a signal from a finite set of time-domain samples. It takes measured data — a discrete sequence of N samples — and maps it to a spectral representation, trading frequency resolution against variance via its tuning parameters: the window length (longer windows give finer resolution but higher variance; shorter windows do the reverse), the window function (rectangular, Hann, Hamming, Bartlett — each shapes the spectral leakage profile), and the estimation method (periodogram, averaged periodogram via Welch or Bartlett, parametric models such as autoregressive fitting, or subspace approaches like MUSIC). The technique persists through published algorithms (Bartlett 1948, Welch 1967), software implementations embedded in every signal-processing toolkit (MATLAB, SciPy, GNU Radio), and the standard operating procedure of engineers who must decide whether a signal contains tones, noise, or broadband energy when only a finite record is available. [formal: estimatio spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A welch-method estimate of a signal's power spectral density is produced by dividing a finite-length discrete signal into M non-overlapping (or optionally overlapping with 50% overlap) segments of equal length L, applying a window function (typically Hann or Hamming) to each segment to reduce spectral leakage, computing the periodogram of each windowed segment via the discrete Fourier transform, and averaging those M periodograms to produce a smoothed spectral estimate with lower variance than a single periodogram at the cost of reduced frequency resolution. The technique's parameters are the segment length L (controlling resolution), the number of segments M (controlling variance reduction as variance scales as 1/M), and the overlap ratio (0 for non-overlapping, up to 0.5 or 0.75 for partial overlap, trading resolution back against the segment count). It persists through the original 1967 Welch paper, every major signal-processing library (MATLAB's pwelch, SciPy's welch, GNU Radio's spectrum block), and the standard engineering practice of computing spectral estimates from real-world finite data where raw periodograms prove too noisy for practical use. [formal: methodus welchiana | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A filter-bank is a human-made signal processing construct consisting of a parallel array of band-pass filters, each tuned to a distinct frequency band, that decompose an input signal into its constituent spectral components by routing each band through its dedicated filter channel. The architecture's parameters are the number of bands (linear spacing, logarithmic/mel spacing, or constant-Q spacing), the center frequencies and bandwidths of each bandpass element, the filter order and type (FIR, IIR, polyphase), and the implementation structure (cascade, parallel lattice, or FFT-based polyphase decomposition). The bank persists through hardware implementations (analog filter arrays in RF receivers, digital FIR/IIR filter banks in software-defined radio), standardized perceptual filter banks (the 26-band mel filter bank used in speech processing and the MFCC pipeline, the 40-band gammatone filter bank modeling cochlear frequency resolution), and embedded DSP libraries (Intel IPP, ARM NEON filter-bank kernels). The removal test distinguishes filter-bank operation from its components: removing any single band's filter collapses that band's channel but leaves the rest of the bank operational, while removing the bank structure eliminates the simultaneous multi-band decomposition entirely. [formal: grex filtrorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

A spectrum-analyzer is a measurement instrument that converts a time-domain input signal into its frequency-domain representation, displaying amplitude (or power) as a function of frequency. It operates by either (1) sweeping a tunable band-pass filter across the frequency range and measuring output magnitude at each center frequency, or (2) digitizing the signal and applying a fast Fourier transform (FFT) with configurable windowing and averaging parameters to produce a spectral plot. The display persists on screen or is stored for later analysis. [formal: spectrum-analyzer | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A band-pass-filter is a signal processing construct that passes signals within a specific frequency range (defined by a lower cutoff frequency f_L and an upper cutoff frequency f_H) while attenuating frequencies outside that band. Its behavior is fully specified by three parameters: the center frequency f_C = sqrt(f_L · f_H), the bandwidth BW = f_H − f_L, and the quality factor Q = f_C / BW, which determines selectivity. It persists through two implementations: analog circuits (RLC networks, active filters with op-amps) and digital algorithms (FIR/IIR filter designs such as butterworth, chebyshev, or elliptic). A signal that survives the band without significant amplitude loss is said to be in the passband; everything else falls in the stopband.
[formal: band-pass-filter | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mel-frequency-spectrogram is a time-frequency representation of a signal constructed in three steps: (1) partition the signal into overlapping frames using a window function, (2) compute the periodogram (or Welch estimate) for each frame to obtain a linear-frequency spectrogram, (3) map the linear frequency bins to mel-scale bins by summing energy contributions according to a triangular mel-filterbank. The result is a 2-D representation with time on one axis and perceptually-spaced frequency on the other. The parameters are the frame size, hop length, window type, and the number of mel bins; persistence is through standard DSP libraries (librosa, kaldi, matlab) that implement the full pipeline as a deterministic transformation. [formal: mel-spectrogram | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cepstral-envelope is the smooth, coarse spectral shape extracted from a cepstrum by isolating the low-quefrency components — the part of the quefrency-domain representation that captures the slowly varying structure of a signal. It is computed by applying a low-pass filter or smoothing operation to the cepstrum, thereby separating the slowly-varying envelope (associated with vocal-tract or source-filter characteristics) from the rapidly-varying fine structure (associated with excitation details or noise). The cepstral-envelope persists as a feature vector derived algorithmically from the cepstrum, which itself is computed from a signal via logarithmic power-spectrum FFT. The parameters defining it are: (1) the cepstrum as input, (2) the low-quefrency cutoff or smoothing bandwidth that determines the separation threshold between envelope and fine structure, and (3) the signal from which the cepstrum was originally derived. [formal: involucrum-cepstrale | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cross-correlation is a mathematical operation that computes the similarity between two signals x(t) and y(t) as a function of a time lag τ applied to one signal: R_xy(τ) = ∫ x(t)·y*(t-τ) dt (continuous) or R_xy[τ] = Σ x[n]·y*[n-τ] (discrete). It operates by sliding one signal past another, computing an overlap integral or sum at each lag, producing a cross-correlogram that reveals delay, periodicity, and matching patterns. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic computation over discrete sample arrays or continuous functions, implemented via direct summation or FFT-based convolution. [formal: cross-correlation | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A spectral peak is a local maximum in the magnitude spectrum of a signal — a frequency bin whose spectral amplitude exceeds that of its neighboring bins above a specified threshold. The parameters that carve a spectral peak are: (1) a spectral representation (magnitude versus frequency), (2) a peak-finding algorithm or threshold rule that identifies local maxima, and (3) a minimum-separation constraint to distinguish resolved peaks from spectral leakage. A spectral peak persists as a computational construct encoded in peak-detection algorithms (e.g., argmax with windowing, local-maxima search with noise-floor gating) and is sustained through standard signal-processing toolchains (FFT analysis, audio feature extraction, radar signal processing) where it serves as a primitive for pitch detection, spectral-envelope estimation, event classification, and tonal content analysis. [formal: climax | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mel-frequency scale is a perceptual frequency scale used in audio signal processing and psychoacoustics that approximates human pitch perception. It maps physical frequency in hertz to mel units using the transformation: mel = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700), where f is the frequency in Hz. Below 1000 Hz the scale is approximately linear with a slope of ~1 mel/Hz; above 1000 Hz it becomes logarithmic, reflecting the ear's diminishing frequency resolution. The scale is defined by three parameters: (1) the reference formula mapping Hz to mels, (2) the inflection point at 1000 Hz where linearity gives way to logarithmic compression, and (3) the normalization constants (2595 and 700) derived from empirical psychoacoustic experiments by Stevens, Volkmann, and Newman (1937) and later refined by Steinberg and Palmer (1993). It persists through standardization in audio toolkits (Librosa, HTK, Praat), speech recognition frameworks, and music information retrieval systems as a reusable perceptual mapping. [formal: mel | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Frequency warping is a technique in audio signal processing that transforms frequencies from one scale to another through a monotonic mapping function. The most common form maps physical frequencies in hertz to perceptual frequency scales such as the mel scale or Bark scale, where equal distances in the target scale correspond to equal perceived pitch differences. The transform is typically defined as a piecewise linear or smooth function f: Hz → target-scale that preserves ordering while compressing higher frequencies to match human auditory resolution. The method persists through algorithmic specifications embedded in audio processing software, mathematical formulations in signal processing literature, and implementation as lookup tables or analytic functions in real-time audio systems. [formal: freq-warp | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The discrete-cosine-transform (DCT) is a linear invertible transform that maps a real-valued input sequence x[n] of length N into real-valued coefficients X[k] via the formula X[k] = sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x[n] * cos(pi/N * (n + 0.5) * k), for k = 0..N-1. It comes in four standard types (DCT-I through DCT-IV); DCT-II is the most widely used variant, forming the core of DCT-based compression. The transform concentrates signal energy into a small number of low-frequency coefficients, enabling efficient quantization and entropy coding. Persistence: implemented as algorithms in software libraries (FFTW, LAPACK), hardware DSP blocks, and standardized in codecs (MPEG, ITU-T). [formal: dct | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral decomposition is a mathematical technique that represents a signal or function as a sum of basis functions indexed by frequency. The input is a time-domain or spatial-domain signal x(t); the output is a frequency-domain representation X(f) where each coefficient encodes the amplitude and phase of a specific frequency component. The mechanism of persistence is mathematical notation (Fourier series, Fourier transform, spectral factorization), algorithmic implementations (discrete Fourier transform, fast Fourier transform, eigenvalue decomposition for matrices), and software libraries across signal processing and scientific computing. [formal: decompisitionem spectrum | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) is a time-frequency analysis technique. Parameters: (1) window size — the length of each segment in samples; (2) window type — the tapering function (Hann, Hamming, Blackman, etc.) applied to reduce spectral leakage at segment boundaries; (3) hop size or overlap — the step between consecutive window positions, controlling time resolution. The STFT operates by multiplying the input signal by a sliding window, computing the FFT of each windowed segment, and recording the complex spectrum at each time step, producing a 2D representation of signal energy across time and frequency. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic computation: the STFT is a deterministic mathematical transform that can be computed from any discrete-time signal given the three parameters, and its results are stored as a time-frequency matrix. [formal: stft | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A cepstral lifter is a filter operating in the quefrency (cepstral) domain. Parameters: (1) lifter type — low-pass (extracts spectral envelope by preserving low-quefrency coefficients), high-pass (extracts residual/excitation by preserving high-quefrency coefficients), band-pass (isolates a quefrency band), or notch (removes a specific quefrency component); (2) cutoff quefrency — the quefrency threshold that separates passband from stopband; (3) lifter shape — the functional form of attenuation in the stopband (rectangular, exponential, cosine-tapered). The lifter works by applying a window function to the cepstral coefficients, optionally zeroing out selected quefrency bins, then transforming back to the frequency domain via IDFT. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic computation: the lifter is a deterministic operation on cepstral coefficients that can be applied to any signal representation that has been cepstrally analyzed, and its output is a modified spectrum or time-domain signal. [formal: cepstral-lifter | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral-feature is a numerical descriptor extracted from a signal's spectral representation that captures a measurable aspect of its frequency-domain structure. Parameters: (1) source domain — the spectral representation from which the feature is derived (power spectrum, cepstrum, or spectrogram); (2) computation — the specific mathematical operation used to extract the scalar or vector value (e.g., weighted mean for spectral centroid, cepstral coefficients for MFCCs, percentile for rolloff); (3) dimensionality — whether the result is a single scalar or a vector of values. Persistence mechanism: standardized mathematical definitions used in signal processing, audio engineering, and machine learning. [formal: characteristicum-spectrale | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

Pitch-detection is a computational technique that estimates the fundamental frequency (F0) of a periodic or quasi-periodic signal, most commonly audio or speech. Parameters: (1) input signal — the waveform or its spectral representation (STFT, cepstrum, or raw); (2) algorithm class — autocorrelation, cepstral, FFT-based, hybrid, or learning-based methods; (3) detectable range — the frequency band the method covers (e.g., 50–5000 Hz for human voice and music); (4) output resolution — the precision of the frequency estimate in Hertz or cents. Persistence: implemented as software libraries and hardware modules in music synthesis, speech recognition, audio analysis, and music information retrieval systems; taught as a core concept in DSP and audio engineering curricula; sustained by active research in computational musicology and speech processing. Cepstral-coefficients is a sequence of numerical values obtained from cepstral analysis, representing the amplitude characteristics of a signal in the quefrency domain. Parameters: (1) the number of coefficients (typically 12–26 for speech, encoding the spectral envelope), (2) the window length and hop size used in the underlying short-time Fourier transform, (3) the frequency warping scale (e.g., mel or linear). Persistence: through standardized feature extraction algorithms in speech and audio processing toolkits (HTK, Kaldi, librosa), their use as input feature vectors in automatic speech recognition and audio classification systems, and their mathematical definition via the cepstrum transform (Bogert, Healy, and Tukey, 1963). [formal: coefficientes cepstrales | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Furniture comprises human-made, movable objects designed to support specific human activities — sitting, sleeping, storing, working, eating — through engineered form-function relationships. Parameters: (1) a physical artifact designed for human use rather than production or consumption; (2) a function class (seating, surface, storage, sleeping, decorative); (3) material construction chosen for structural integrity and aesthetic fit. Persistence mechanism: manufacturing traditions, design standards, and cultural knowledge are transmitted through education, trade catalogs, and retail practice, maintaining a stable taxonomy of furniture types across generations. The concept persists because human dwellings and public spaces require standardized solution patterns for recurring activities.

Liftering is a signal processing technique that applies a window function to the cepstrum in the quefrency domain to selectively modify frequency components. Procedure: compute cepstrum via FFT of log-power spectrum; multiply cepstrum by a window function (low-pass, high-pass, or band-pass) in quefrency domain; reconstruct signal by inverse FFT of the exponentiated windowed cepstrum. Parameters: lifter shape, quefrency range, window type (Hanning, Hamming, rectangular). Persistence: codified in Oppenheim and Schafer Discrete-Time Signal Processing; implemented in DSP libraries (MATLAB, Python SciPy, librosa). [formal: liftering | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.86]

The cepstral-transform is the algorithmic procedure that maps a time-domain signal to the quefrency domain. Procedure: given input signal x[n], compute X[k] = FFT(x[n]); take log magnitude L[k] = log|X[k]|; compute c[n] = IDFT(L[k]) to obtain the cepstrum. Parameters include FFT size, zero-padding, and optional windowing of the input. Persists as a standardized algorithm encoded in signal processing libraries and textbooks. [formal: transformus cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral subtraction is a noise reduction technique that estimates the power spectrum of additive noise (from noise-only segments or clean speech segments), subtracts this noise estimate from the noisy signal spectrum using an over-subtraction factor, applies a spectral floor to avoid negative values, and reconstructs the cleaned signal via inverse FFT. Parameters: noise estimation method, over-subtraction factor (typically 1-4x), spectral floor level. [formal: subtractio spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral-transform is the computational procedure that converts a time-domain signal into its cepstral representation. It operates by: (1) computing the power spectral density of the input signal via FFT, (2) taking the logarithm of the spectrum, and (3) applying an inverse FFT to produce the quefrency-domain output (cepstral coefficients). The transform persists as a deterministic algorithmic pipeline. [formal: transformus cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral-envelope is the slowly-varying amplitude profile extracted from cepstral coefficients by applying low-pass liftering (quefrency-domain windowing). It captures the gross spectral shape of a signal — notably the vocal tract characteristic in speech — by suppressing rapid quefrency variations (glottal pulse structure). Parameters: input = cepstral coefficient sequence, window = low-pass lifter in quefrency domain, output = smoothed envelope sequence. Persists as a deterministic filtering operation on discrete quefrency samples. [formal: envelope cepstralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Noise-reduction is a category of signal processing techniques that estimate the statistical properties of additive noise and apply a transformation to attenuate the noise component while preserving the desired signal. Key parameters: (1) noise estimation strategy (noise-only segments, statistical modeling, or spectral gating), (2) attenuation function (spectral subtraction, Wiener gain, soft thresholding), (3) signal domain (time, frequency, cepstral). Persistence mechanism: mathematical algorithms implemented in software or hardware DSP systems. [formal: reductio-inquinamenti | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A perceptual frequency scale in hertz, designed to model human auditory perception, where equal-distance steps are perceived as equal pitch intervals. The mel scale maps linear frequency f (in Hz) to perceived pitch m via the formula m = 2595 · log₁₀(1 + f/700). It was developed by Stevens, Volkmann, and Newman (1937) as part of their psychophysical experiments on pitch discrimination. The scale compresses high frequencies (where human pitch discrimination is coarser) relative to low frequencies (where discrimination is finer). It persists through its use in the design of mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs), mel-filter banks, and mel-scaled spectrograms — the standard representation for speech recognition, music information retrieval, and audio classification systems. [formal: mel-frequency | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.11]

Bit-rate is the quantitative measure of the rate at which bits are processed, transmitted, stored, or generated per unit of time, expressed in bits per second (bps) and its multiples (kbps, Mbps, Gbps). Parameters include the measurement mode (instantaneous, average, or peak), the bit classification (payload only, or total including protocol overhead and error-correction bits), and the time window over which the rate is computed. The persistence mechanism is the standardized unit and specification embedded in telecommunications protocols (ITU-T, IEEE), digital media encoding standards (MPEG, AAC, H.26x), and networking equipment to define, negotiate, and enforce data rates. [formal: bit-rate | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

A phoneme is the smallest abstract unit of sound in a given language such that substituting one phoneme for another in a word changes the word's meaning (minimal pair distinction). Parameters include: the language or dialect to which the phoneme system belongs, the inventory of phonemes (typically 20-100 sounds per language), the distinctive features that differentiate phonemes (voicing, place and manner of articulation for consonants; height, backness, roundedness for vowels), and the allophonic variants (context-dependent phonetic realizations of the same phoneme). The persistence mechanism is the phonological theory and classification system codified in descriptive grammars, the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA) chart, language documentation projects, and phonetic transcription standards used in linguistics, computational language processing, and speech recognition systems. A mel-spectrogram is a time-frequency representation that maps a signal's spectral energy onto the mel frequency scale, producing a 2D array with time on one axis and mel-frequency bins on the other. Parameters include: the frame size and hop length (determining temporal resolution), the number of mel bins (determining frequency resolution), the window function applied to each frame (typically Hann or Hamming), and whether log scaling is applied to the resulting energies. The persistence mechanism is software implementations in standard libraries (librosa, TensorFlow Audio, PyTorch torchaudio) and their integration into machine learning pipelines for speech recognition, audio classification, and music information retrieval. [formal: spectrum mel | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

Linear Predictive Coding (LPC) models a digital signal (originally speech) as the output of a linear filter driven by an excitation source. For each sample s(n), the technique predicts the value as a weighted sum of p past samples: s̃(n) = Σ(aᵢ · s(n-i)) for i=1..p, where aᵢ are the prediction coefficients and p is the prediction order. The residual (actual minus predicted) captures the excitation source's characteristics (pitch periodicity and timbre), while the filter coefficients model the signal's spectral envelope. The coefficients are computed by minimizing the prediction error, yielding the Yule-Walker equations solved via the Levinson-Durbin recursion on the signal's autocorrelation matrix. Parameters: prediction order (p, typically 8-16 for speech at 8 kHz), prediction coefficients (aᵢ, encoding the spectral envelope), residual signal (the excitation). Persistence mechanism: standardized algorithm embedded in codec specifications (ITU-T G.729, 3GPP AMR, GSM Full Rate), implemented in hardware DSP chips and software libraries across telecommunications, audio coding, and pitch estimation systems since the 1960s. [formal: linearis praedictio codificatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral-distance is a measure of dissimilarity between two spectral shapes, computed from the cepstral coefficients of each spectrum. The most common form is the Itakura-Saito distance, the cepstral Euclidean distance, or the Mahalanobis distance computed on cepstral vectors. Given two spectra represented as cepstral coefficient vectors c1 and c2, the distance d(c1,c2) quantifies their spectral envelope divergence, enabling applications in speaker recognition, speech quality assessment, and material classification. The metric persists as a mathematical formula implemented in speech processing and audio analysis software. [formal: distantia cepstralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mathematical signal processing technique that represents a signal as a superposition of wavelets — functions localized in both time and frequency. Given a mother wavelet ψ(t), the continuous wavelet transform computes C(a,b) = ∫f(t)ψ*((t-b)/a)/√|a| dt for scale a>0 and shift b∈ℝ; the discrete variant uses dyadic scales (a=2^j) and shifts (b=k·2^j) for computational efficiency. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic: the transform is computed via filter banks (Mallat's pyramid algorithm) or direct convolution, and the resulting coefficients encode signal structure across resolutions. [formal: transformatio waveletica | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A music-theory concept that groups all pitches sharing the same pitch name into a single equivalence class, abstracting away octave and timbre. Developed within 20th-century atonal theory (Schoenberg, Forte), it serves as the foundation for pitch-class set theory, where sets of pitch classes (called pitch-class sets) are analyzed by their interval content. Pitch classes are typically numbered 0–11 (C=0, C#=1, ..., B=11). [formal: classis-tonalis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

A frequency scale that transforms linear Hertz values to a perceptual mel scale using the formula m = 2595 × log₁₀(1 + f/700), where f is frequency in Hz. The scale approximates the human auditory system's non-linear frequency resolution and persists through computational implementations in audio processing toolkits and standardization in speech and audio analysis pipelines. [formal: mel-frequency-scaled | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A signal processing framework that represents a signal jointly in time and frequency dimensions, producing a two-dimensional distribution that reveals how spectral content evolves. It operates through parameterized transforms — short-time Fourier transform (STFT) with windowed spectral slices, continuous wavelet transform with scale-time scaling, and quadratic forms like the Wigner-Ville distribution — each trading off resolution between time and frequency per the uncertainty principle. The persistence mechanism is mathematical algorithms implemented as signal processing software and hardware, standardized across engineering disciplines since the 1940s. [formal: repraesentatio temporis-frequentialis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A chroma representation (also called a chromagram) is a 12-dimensional feature vector that encodes the energy distribution across the 12 pitch classes of the equal-tempered scale (C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#, A, A#, B). It is computed by transforming a short-time Fourier spectrum through a chroma filterbank that folds all octaves into a single octave, producing an octave-invariant representation. The chroma vector is the result of applying a 12-row kernel that sums spectral energy at harmonics of each pitch class. Chroma features are widely used for chord recognition, key detection, music similarity comparison, and timbral analysis because they abstract away pitch height while preserving harmonic content. The representation trades frequency resolution for octave invariance, making it robust to transposition but losing fine-grained spectral detail. [formal: chroma | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A frequency-scale is a human-made mapping function that transforms a linear frequency axis into a perceptually or structurally organized scale, specifying both the transformation formula and the fixed parameters (coefficients, reference values) that determine the mapping. A frequency-scale is a human-made mapping function that converts a linear frequency axis to a perceptually or structurally organized scale, defined by a precise transformation formula and fixed coefficients. It persists through published standards, reference DSP implementations, and the conventions they establish for audio analysis.
