A parametric model is a human-made mathematical framework that represents data, signals, or phenomena using a fixed set of parameters whose values are optimized to fit observed measurements according to a specified criterion. It persists through formal algorithms (least squares, maximum likelihood, etc.), published parameter-estimation methods, and standardized model families (AR, MA, ARMA, state-space) that define both the structural form and the fitting procedure. [formal: modelium parametricum | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A spectral reconstruction technique takes a compact or partial spectral representation (magnitude-only spectra, quantized coefficients, or downsampled bins) and recovers a full complex-valued spectrum. It operates by iterating between spectral magnitude constraints and an initial phase guess, updating via inverse short-time Fourier transform, applying a time-domain window, and re-transforming — converging when the reconstructed spectrum matches the input magnitude within tolerance. Persistence mechanism: iterative optimization algorithms (Griffin-Lim, iterated Griffin-Lim, vocoder-based phase recovery) implemented in signal processing libraries and audio codecs. [formal: reconstructio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.01]

Envelope extraction isolates the slow-varying amplitude contour of a signal by computing its short-time spectral magnitude, finding local maxima across successive frames, and smoothing the peak trajectory with a low-pass filter or moving average. It operates on the principle that envelope changes are orders of magnitude slower than carrier oscillations. Persistence mechanism: peak-tracking algorithms (half-wave rectification + low-pass filtering, Hilbert transform analytic signal, Viterbi trellis tracking) implemented in DSP libraries and speech processing toolkits. [formal: extrahatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.02]

Mel-frequency cepstral coefficients (MFCCs) transform a signal's short-time Fourier spectrum into a compact representation of vocal tract characteristics. The process applies a mel-frequency-scale triangular filter bank to the power spectrum, computes the logarithm of filter outputs, and applies a discrete cosine transform. Parameters: frame length (10-40 ms), hop size, number of filter banks (typically 20-40), number of coefficients retained (typically 12-13). Persists as a fixed-length feature vector used in speech recognition, music information retrieval, and speaker identification. [formal: mfccs | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The constant-Q transform decomposes a signal into frequency bins whose bandwidth is proportional to center frequency, yielding a log-frequency time-frequency representation with constant quality factor Q. The analysis window length increases inversely with frequency: narrow bandwidth at low frequencies, wide at high. Parameters: number of octaves, bins per octave, reference frequency, quality factor Q. Persists as a spectrogram-like representation where frequency resolution follows a logarithmic scale, naturally suited to musical signal analysis where perceptual pitch resolution is logarithmic. [formal: constant-q-transform | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Audio restoration is the algorithmic repair of degraded audio signals. The technique analyzes corrupted audio (noisy, clipped, bandwidth-limited, or physically damaged) and applies signal processing operations — spectral subtraction, de-essing, de-clicking, equalization, and noise gating — to recover the original signal or improve perceptual quality. The persistence mechanism is implementation as executable DSP routines in audio editing and archival software. [formal: audio-restauratio | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

Amplitude-analysis is the extraction and quantification of a signal's amplitude characteristics. It operates by computing envelope curves via rectification and low-pass filtering, measuring peak amplitudes, and deriving root-mean-square (RMS) energy values. The persistence mechanism is a set of deterministic mathematical operations implemented in digital signal processors and software libraries. It carves the boundary between raw signal amplitude and derived amplitude metrics, enabling signal characterization across audio, communications, and instrumentation domains. [formal: amplitude-analysis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Phase-retrieval is the reconstruction of phase information from magnitude-only observations — an inverse problem solved by imposing constraints across domains. It operates through iterative algorithms (Gerchberg-Saxton, Griffin-Lim) that alternate between the measurement domain and a constraint domain (support, non-negativity, known magnitude), or through modern convex relaxation and learning-based methods. It persists as mathematical theory, algorithmic implementations, and applied practice across signal processing, X-ray crystallography, and astronomical imaging. [formal: recuperatio phasei | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.60]

Fundamental frequency (F0) is the lowest frequency of a periodic waveform, representing the rate at which the sound source repeats its cycle. In speech, it corresponds to vocal fold vibration rate; in music, to the perceived pitch of tonal sounds. F0 is estimated through time-domain methods (autocorrelation, average amplitude difference) or frequency-domain methods (cepstral analysis, spectral peak picking). The concept picks out the fundamental from its harmonics (integer multiples), and persists through estimation algorithms (YIN, SWIPE, pYIN), prosodic annotation frameworks (ToBI), and pitch-tracking conventions in signal processing toolkits. [formal: fundamental frequency | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral entropy is a scalar measure computed from the normalized power distribution across a signal's frequency bins, treating the distribution as a probability mass function and applying the Shannon entropy formula. It quantifies the uniformity of spectral energy: low entropy indicates tonal, concentrated spectra; high entropy indicates noise-like, distributed spectra. Persistence mechanism: computed algorithmically from digitized signals; stored as numerical features in analysis pipelines and classification systems. [formal: entropyia spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

Spectral tilt is the overall slope of a signal's power spectral density across frequency, typically expressed in decibels per octave. It quantifies how rapidly energy decreases (or increases) as frequency rises — a steep negative tilt indicates energy concentrated in lower frequencies (bass-heavy), while a flatter or positive tilt indicates energy distributed toward higher frequencies. Computed as the linear regression slope of the log-power spectrum versus log-frequency, or approximated as the ratio of low-band to high-band energy. Used to characterize voice quality (breathiness, vocal fry), instrument timbre, and environmental acoustics. [formal: spectri inclinis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Delta cepstral coefficients are computed by estimating the temporal derivative of cepstral coefficient sequences using a finite slope filter. Given a window of N cepstral frames centered at time t, the delta coefficient for each cepstral dimension d is calculated as the slope of a least-squares linear fit: δ_d(t) = Σ_{n=-k}^{k} n·c_d(t+n) / Σ_{n=-k}^{k} n², where c_d is the coefficient value for dimension d, k = ⌊(N−1)/2⌋, and the summation runs over the symmetric window. The filter weights are fixed and normalized to preserve the dynamic range of the original coefficients. This computation is deterministic and runs in O(k) time per frame per coefficient dimension. [formal: delta | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral mean normalization (CMN) is a signal processing technique that computes the frame-wise mean of cepstral coefficient vectors across a speech utterance and subtracts this mean from each frame, thereby removing channel-induced spectral distortions and stabilizing speaker-independent recognition. Parameters: the mean is computed per coefficient dimension across all frames in the utterance (or a sliding window); the subtraction is applied element-wise to each frame's coefficient vector. Persistence mechanism: implemented as an algorithm in speech recognition front-ends, encoded in audio processing libraries (Python, MATLAB), and taught as a standard preprocessing step in speech processing curricula. [formal: latin | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A memory encoding technique in which information is systematically associated with elements of an imagined spatial environment — a route, building, or palace. The rememberer visualizes navigating this space and encounters each designated location in sequence, with each location bound to one piece of information through vivid imagery. Recall proceeds by mentally traversing the route and retrieving the bound information at each stop. The technique exploits human spatial memory, which is evolutionarily and cognitively more robust than verbal or numerical memory alone, and converts arbitrary information into spatially anchored, navigable form. [formal: methodus locorum | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A psychoacoustic frequency scale that maps physical sound frequency in hertz to perceived critical-band number on a 0–24 scale. The conversion is defined by the Zwicker formula: z = 13·arctan(0.00076·f) + 3.5·arctan((f/7500)^2), where z is the bark value and f is the frequency in Hz. The scale divides the audible spectrum into 24 critical bands, each representing the frequency resolution of the human auditory system at that region. Persistence mechanism: the mathematical mapping is codified in psychoacoustic literature and international audio standards (ITU-R BS.516, ISO 532), maintained through engineering practice and computational libraries. [formal: bark | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An iterative phase-recovery algorithm that reconstructs a time-domain signal from a magnitude spectrogram. It alternates between inverse-STFT to estimate phase, forward-STFT to enforce the magnitude constraint, and repeats until the error between the estimated and target magnitude spectrogram falls below a convergence threshold. The algorithm is deterministic given the same initialization and parameters. Parameters: magnitude spectrogram input, maximum iteration count, convergence tolerance, and initial phase guess. Persistence mechanism: implemented in signal-processing libraries (librosa, MATLAB, Python scipy), documented in peer-reviewed literature, and used in audio synthesis and speech processing pipelines. [formal: Griffin-Lim | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The number of samples between consecutive analysis frames in windowed-overlap-add processing such as the short-time Fourier transform. It determines the overlap ratio between successive windows and controls the trade-off between time resolution and spectral smearing. Key parameters: sample rate, frame size, and resulting overlap percentage. Persistence mechanism: defined as a standard parameter in signal processing theory, implemented in audio libraries (librosa, MATLAB, scipy), and used in speech recognition and audio analysis pipelines. [formal: hop-size | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A chroma feature (chromagram) represents spectral energy as a 12-dimensional vector, one value per chroma (pitch class C through B), obtained by applying a pitch-class profile to a spectrogram and summing energy within each class. Computed via a 12-band filter bank applied to the magnitude spectrum, then normalized to [0,1]. Persisted as a fixed-length numeric array in music analysis pipelines. The construction is deterministic: given a signal, windowed-STFT, and equal-tempered pitch mapping, the chroma vector is uniquely determined. [formal: chroma | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A pitch-class-profile is a 12-element filter bank used to compute chroma features from a spectrogram. Each element is a kernel function (typically Gaussian) centered on the frequency of one pitch class in the 12-tone equal-tempered scale: f_c = 440 * 2^((n-69)/12) Hz where n is the MIDI note number. Given a spectrogram S(t,f), the pitch-class profile P(t,n) = sum_f S(t,f) * K_n(f) for each pitch class n=0..11, where K_n is the kernel for pitch class n. Persisted as a time-series of 12-dimensional vectors in music information retrieval pipelines. The construction is deterministic and fully specified by the kernel shape, center frequencies, and spectrogram resolution. [formal: pitch_class_profile | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Phase-recovery is the computational process of reconstructing the phase component of a signal's spectrum when only magnitude (or magnitude and partial phase) information is available. Its parameters are: (1) an input magnitude spectrum (or magnitude with incomplete phase), (2) an iterative or direct reconstruction algorithm (e.g., Griffin-Lim, spectral conversion via Hilbert transform, or neural phase synthesis), and (3) a convergence criterion or fixed iteration count. It persists through the discipline of audio signal processing, embedded in phase vocoders, speech synthesis pipelines, and music information retrieval systems. [formal: recuperatio-phasei | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A phase-vocoder is an audio signal processing technique that modifies the time-scale and/or pitch of a signal by manipulating its short-time Fourier transform (STFT) representation. Its parameters are: (1) a window function (typically Hann) for analysis and synthesis, (2) a hop-size for frame extraction, (3) a phase progression model (initially linear extrapolation from consecutive STFT frames), (4) magnitude and phase spectra as input, and (5) an inverse STFT for resynthesis. Its persistence mechanism: the algorithm iterates over successive frames, computing magnitude and phase spectra via windowed DFT, modifying phase according to a predicted linear progression (plus corrections for phase unwrapping), applying time-scale or pitch modification factors to the phase and magnitude, then reconstructing the time-domain signal via overlap-add of windowed inverse DFT frames. [formal: phase-vocoder | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The mel-frequency-cepstrum is a representation of a signal's spectral envelope warped onto the mel scale, a perceptual frequency scale where equal distances sound equally spaced to human ears. It is computed by: (1) applying a windowed Fourier transform (STFT) to obtain the power spectrum; (2) mapping the spectrum frequencies to the mel scale using triangular overlapping windows; (3) taking the logarithm of the mel-spectrum energies; (4) applying a discrete cosine transform to produce the cepstral coefficients. The mel-warped representation captures the timbral structure of speech and audio more faithfully than linear-frequency cepstra for human-centered applications. [formal: mfc | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

Pitch tracking is a signal processing technique that estimates the fundamental frequency (F0) of an audio signal as a time-varying function, producing a pitch contour. The method operates by analyzing short time frames of the audio — typically using autocorrelation, cepstral analysis, or combined time-and-frequency approaches — to detect periodicity and extract the dominant pitch at each frame. The output is a sequence of frequency values over time, representing how pitch evolves across a speech or musical signal. Persistence occurs through algorithmic implementations in software, standardized test protocols, and established practice in music and speech processing. [formal: investigatio toni | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

A windowing function is a family of mathematical functions (e.g. Hamming, Hann, Blackman, Gaussian) that multiply a signal segment to taper its amplitude toward the edges of the analysis frame, thereby reducing spectral leakage in discrete Fourier transform analysis. The function is defined by a closed-form expression or lookup table, instantiated as numerical coefficients in DSP software and signal processing libraries. [formal: functio | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

A log-magnitude-spectrum is the base-10 logarithmic transformation of a magnitude spectrum, computed as 10·log₁₀(|X(f)|²) where X(f) is the frequency-domain representation of a signal segment. It converts multiplicative convolution in the time domain (e.g. source-filter separation in speech) into additive decomposition, enabling linear modeling of spectral envelope. The transformation is implemented as a mathematical operation within DSP pipelines and audio analysis software. [formal: log-magnitudo-spectrum | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Dynamic-range-compression is an audio processing technique that reduces the difference between the loudest and quietest parts of an audio signal. It operates by measuring the signal's amplitude envelope and applying variable gain: when the signal exceeds a threshold, gain is reduced according to a compression ratio. The technique is controlled by four parameters — threshold (the amplitude level at which compression begins), ratio (the amount of reduction applied), attack time (how quickly compression engages), and release time (how quickly it disengages). The persistence mechanism is the compressor algorithm itself, implemented in analog circuits (vacuum tubes, VCA), digital signal processors, or software plugins, enduring across music production, broadcasting, film audio, and speech processing workflows. [formal: compressio dynamic-range | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A mel-frequency-spectrum is a time-frequency representation that maps the linear frequency axis of a magnitude spectrum onto the mel scale — a perceptual frequency scale where equal distances correspond to equal perceived pitch intervals. It is computed by (1) applying a triangular filterbank spaced evenly on the mel scale to the magnitude spectrum, and (2) retaining the filterbank output as a sequence of mel-frequency coefficients indexed by time and mel-band. The persistence mechanism is the filterbank transform itself, which is deterministic and reproducible: any implementation of the mel-spaced triangular filterbank applied to a magnitude spectrum produces the same output. [formal: spectrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Chroma features are a digital audio representation that projects a signal's spectral energy onto the 12 pitch classes of the Western equal-tempered scale, producing a 12-dimensional vector invariant under octave transposition. The representation is carved by (1) the 12-tone chromatic partition, (2) the octave-invariance constraint, and (3) the spectral projection operation that folds frequency bins onto pitch-class bins. It persists in audio analysis software, music information retrieval systems, and symbolic representations of tonal harmony. [formal: chroma | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.41]

Onset detection is a signal processing technique that identifies temporal points where acoustic events begin, by computing a feature function (typically an energy envelope or spectral flux) and locating local maxima above a dynamic threshold. The method operates by: (1) extracting a time-varying energy or spectral feature from the signal, (2) differentiating the feature to emphasise changes, and (3) applying a threshold — fixed or adaptive — to mark candidate onsets, followed by post-processing to remove duplicates. Persistence mechanism: implemented as algorithms in digital audio workstations, beat-tracking systems, and music information retrieval libraries; taught as a standard technique in signal processing curricula. [formal: onset-detectio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Beat tracking is a music information retrieval technique that determines the temporal positions of perceptual beats in musical audio. The method operates by: (1) extracting an onset function from the audio signal, (2) computing a beat-synchronous representation or autocorrelation of the onset sequence, (3) estimating the tempo from periodicity peaks, and (4) aligning beat positions to the estimated tempo using dynamic programming or Viterbi decoding. The output is a sequence of beat times synchronized to the music's underlying pulse. Persistence mechanism: implemented in beat-detection algorithms within digital audio workstations, rhythm analysis software, and music information retrieval toolkits; taught as a core technique in MIR curricula. [formal: beat-track | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A spectral transformation that remaps a linear frequency axis (Hertz) onto a non-linear perceptual frequency scale. The transformation applies a monotonic function f(frequency) where the output scale approximates human auditory perception — the mel scale uses f(f) = 2595·log₁₀(1 + f/700), the bark scale uses critical-band boundaries, and the ERB scale uses equivalent rectangular bandwidths. The parameters are the target perceptual scale and the input spectrum; persistence is achieved through standard implementation in DSP libraries and audio processing toolkits. [formal: freq_warping | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral slope is a spectral feature that quantifies the linear trend of spectral energy across frequency bins. It is computed by fitting a straight line to the magnitude spectrum across frequency using least-squares regression, and returns the slope coefficient. A positive slope indicates increasing energy with frequency (brightness); a negative slope indicates decreasing energy. Persistence: computed numerically from discrete magnitude spectra, stored as a single floating-point value per analysis frame. [formal: declivitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Music information retrieval (MIR) is a human-made interdisciplinary field that combines signal processing, machine learning, and musicology to extract structured information from audio signals. It operates by: (1) preprocessing audio through spectral analysis (STFT, windowing), (2) extracting perceptual features (MFCC, chroma, onset, tempo), (3) applying pattern recognition and classification algorithms to identify rhythmic, harmonic, timbral, and structural properties. The field persists through published algorithms, software libraries, acoustic models, and mathematical formulations. [formal: musica informatio recuperanda | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Cepstral coefficients are a representation of the spectral envelope of a signal, obtained by applying a discrete cosine transform to the log power spectrum. They are computed in three stages: (1) compute the power spectrum via Fourier transform, (2) take the logarithm of the power spectrum, (3) apply a discrete cosine transform to produce the coefficients. The first coefficient represents the overall energy, while higher-order coefficients capture the spectral shape. Used extensively in speech recognition and audio analysis for their compact representation of spectral information. [formal: coepstrum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Short-time energy is the measure of signal energy computed over a short, sliding time window (frame) in digital signal processing. It is calculated as the sum of squared amplitude values within each frame: E[n] = Σ x²[m] for m in frame n. It persists through mathematical formulation, software implementations, and standardized audio analysis pipelines. Used in speech processing and music information retrieval for voicing detection, segmentation, and event detection. [formal: energia temporanea brevis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.13]

Spectral peaks are the prominent local maxima identified within a magnitude spectrum, representing the frequency components with the highest energy density. They are computed by detecting local maxima above a noise floor threshold in the frequency domain representation of a signal. Widely used in audio analysis, music information retrieval, and timbre characterization. [formal: spectral_peak | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Phase-estimation is a class of algorithms and methods that recover the phase component of a complex signal (such as a Fourier transform) when only partial phase data or no phase data is available. It operates by imposing constraints — magnitude consistency, phase continuity, temporal smoothness — and iteratively refining phase estimates until convergence. Core parameters: the observed magnitude spectrum or partial phase data as input, the constraint set (non-negativity, band-limitation, support), the iteration count and convergence tolerance, and the initialization strategy. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic procedures encoded in software libraries, mathematical optimization routines, and standardized implementations deployed across audio processing, radar, medical imaging, and telecommunications. [formal: aestimatio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Harmonic-percussive-separation is a signal processing technique that decomposes an audio signal into two additive components: the harmonic part (characterized by sustained tonal content with continuous frequency traces in the time-frequency domain) and the percussive part (characterized by transient, impulsive content with energy spread across frequencies). The method operates on a time-frequency representation (typically a spectrogram or STFT magnitude), applying spectral filtering — low-pass or mask-based approaches for harmonic content, high-pass or residual extraction for percussive content — relying on the spectral sparsity assumption that harmonic and percussive elements rarely overlap in the time-frequency plane. Persistence mechanism: algorithmic procedure encoded in software, applied to digital audio representations. [formal: separatio harmonica-percussiva | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 1.00]

Dither is a digital audio technique that adds a small amount of random noise (typically 1 least-significant-bit amplitude) to a signal before quantization, randomizing the quantization error and converting correlated harmonic distortion into uncorrelated noise with a flat or shaped power spectrum. The technique has two key parameters: (1) noise amplitude, which determines the level of added noise relative to the quantization step, and (2) noise probability distribution, commonly triangular probability density function (TPDF) for noise that spans the quantization range without excess. Dither persists as an algorithmic procedure encoded in digital-to-analog converters, audio recording software, and mastering tools. Without dither, quantization of low-amplitude signals produces audible distortion; with dither, the distortion becomes noise that is perceptually less objectionable. [formal: dithering | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Source-separation is a signal processing technique that decomposes a mixed signal — typically audio containing multiple overlapping sound sources — into individual component sources. The method operates by exploiting differences in spatial position, spectral characteristics, temporal onset patterns, or statistical independence among sources. Common algorithms include Independent Component Analysis (ICA), Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF), and deep learning models trained on labeled source data. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation within software pipelines and hardware systems for music information retrieval, audio engineering, and computational acoustics. [formal: separatio fontium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral-whiteness is an audio analysis metric that quantifies how uniformly acoustic energy is distributed across the frequency spectrum of a signal. It measures the flatness of the power spectral density, with higher values indicating a flatter (whiter) distribution and lower values indicating concentration of energy in specific frequency bands. Computed as the ratio of the geometric mean to the arithmetic mean of the power spectrum across all frequency bins, it serves as a timbral descriptor in music information retrieval for genre classification, instrument recognition, and audio quality assessment. The persistence mechanism is computational: it exists as a derived feature value extracted by analysis software from time-domain audio signals. [formal: albedo spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

An audio feature is a quantifiable property extracted from an audio signal that captures a specific characteristic useful for analysis, classification, or retrieval. Parameters: (1) the feature is derived from a digital audio signal through computational processing; (2) it reduces signal content to a numeric descriptor (scalar, vector, or matrix); (3) it serves downstream tasks such as recognition, segmentation, or similarity measurement. Persistence mechanism: standardized across audio engineering and music information retrieval practice, codified in toolkits (librosa, Essentia,aubio) and academic benchmarks. [formal: audio_feature | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Noise shaping is a digital signal processing technique that modifies the spectral distribution of quantization error by feeding the quantization error through a feedback filter. Parameters: (1) the input signal is quantized at fixed bit depth; (2) the quantization error — the difference between the unquantized and quantized signal — is passed through a shaping filter (typically high-pass or custom); (3) the filtered error is fed back and added to subsequent samples before quantization, creating correlated (colored) noise that pushes energy away from sensitive frequency bands. Persistence mechanism: implemented as digital filter algorithms in DAC firmware, audio processing software, and embedded quantizers; maintained through engineering standards, textbooks, and industry practice in digital audio. [formal: noise_shaping | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

White-noise is a statistical signal model characterized by equal power at all frequencies. Parameters: (1) constant power spectral density across the entire frequency range, (2) zero autocorrelation at all non-zero lags, (3) statistically independent samples drawn from a stationary distribution. The model persists through signal processing theory, communications engineering, and psychoacoustic testing as a baseline reference for system characterization and noise floor analysis. [formal: white_noise | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A model card is a standardized documentation artifact for machine learning models that discloses intended use, performance characteristics, training data provenance, limitations, and ethical considerations. Parameters: (1) structured sections covering model details and performance metrics, (2) demographic or conditional disaggregation where relevant, (3) explicit statements of known limitations and failure modes, (4) governance metadata (authoring team, date, version). Persistence: published as a human-readable document (PDF, HTML, markdown) alongside model repositories, maintained through model iteration cycles, and enforced by organizational policy or regulatory requirement. [formal: model_cardarium | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Tonality is the system by which pitches are organized hierarchically around a central reference (the tonic), with other pitches assigned functional roles (dominant, subdominant, etc.) relative to that center. It operates through three interlocking mechanisms: (1) pitch-class sets that define a scale or mode, (2) functional harmony that assigns gravitational pull between chords, and (3) cadential formulas that articulate tonal closure. The persistence mechanism is explicit teaching through music theory pedagogy, written notation systems, and oral transmission of tonal conventions across generations of musicians and listeners. Tonality is not a natural phenomenon but a cognitive framework humans developed to structure auditory experience into meaningful hierarchical patterns.[formal: tonalitas | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Time-stretching is a signal processing technique that changes the duration of an audio signal while preserving its fundamental pitch. It operates by analyzing the signal into overlapping time frames, manipulating the frame sequencing (inserting or discarding frames), and resynthesizing the output. The method persists through established algorithmic implementations including phase-vocoder overlap-add, time-domain pitch-synchronous overlap-add (TD-PSOLA), and harmonic-percussive separation approaches. It is used in music production, DJ performance, speech processing, and audio analysis. [formal: productio temporis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

Audio-denoising is a class of signal processing techniques that separate desired audio content from unwanted noise by exploiting differences in their statistical, spectral, or temporal properties. Its parameters are: the noise model (stationary vs. transient, additive vs. multiplicative), the preservation targets (speech intelligibility, music fidelity, specific frequency bands), and the algorithmic approach (spectral subtraction, Wiener filtering, wavelet denoising, deep learning-based separation). It persists through implemented algorithms in software libraries (Librosa, TorchAudio, PyTorch), standardized codecs with built-in noise suppression (Opus, WebRTC), and engineering practice in telecommunications, broadcast, and audio post-production — maintained across software versions, documented in signal processing textbooks, and refined through published research. [formal: eliminatio-noise-audio | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Voice-activity-detection (VAD) is a binary classification technique that determines whether a given audio segment contains human speech or non-speech (silence, background noise, music). Its parameters are: the decision threshold (probability cutoff for speech detection), the analysis frame size (typically 10-100ms windows), the feature set used (zero-crossing rate, spectral energy, spectral centroid, MFCCs), and the noise adaptation strategy (static threshold, adaptive threshold, or learned model). It persists through implementations in telephony protocols (SIP, WebRTC), speech recognition front-ends (Kaldi, Mozilla DeepSpeech), embedded voice assistants (Alexa, Google Assistant), and audio recording equipment — maintained through open-source libraries, proprietary SDKs, and engineering practice documented in standards bodies such as ITU-T and 3GPP. [formal: detectio-activitatis-voicalis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Overlap-add is a signal processing technique for reconstructing a full-length signal from overlapping, windowed segments by summing their overlapping contributions. Its parameters are: the analysis window function, the hop size (frame shift between consecutive windows), and the synthesis window (which may be identical to the analysis window). The persistence mechanism is implemented as a mathematical operation in software libraries and digital audio workstations for filter bank reconstruction, STFT-based audio synthesis, and time-domain signal processing. [formal: overlap-add | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The griffin-lim-algorithm is an iterative phase reconstruction technique humans built to estimate the missing phase of a signal's short-time Fourier transform from its magnitude spectrum alone, enabling near-perfect waveform synthesis. Its parameters are: the magnitude spectrum input, the number of iterations, the initialization method for phase, and the convergence criterion. The persistence mechanism is implemented as an algorithm in audio processing software and libraries for speech synthesis and audio restoration. [formal: griffin-lim | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Tonality is the system humans built to organize musical sound around a central reference pitch (the tonic), establishing hierarchies of stability among the remaining pitches and chords. Its parameters are: the tonic pitch, the scale or mode selecting which pitches are in-use versus excluded, and the harmonic grammar governing chord progressions and their functional relationships. It persists through notation systems, tuning conventions, pedagogical tradition, and the cognitive habits of composers and listeners across musical cultures. [formal: tonalitas | substrate: mind | horizon: centuries | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

The discrete cosine transform (DCT) is a mathematical operation humans built to convert a finite sequence of data points into a sum of cosine functions with distinct frequencies and amplitudes. Its parameters are: input length N (power of 2 for efficient computation), transform type (DCT-II being the most common variant used in compression), and normalization scheme. It persists through standardization in image compression (JPEG), audio compression (MP3, AAC), and as a core component in cepstral analysis for speech and audio feature extraction. [formal: discretus cosinus transformatus | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Granular synthesis is a sound synthesis technique in which an audio signal is analyzed, segmented into short overlapping fragments called grains (typically 10–100 milliseconds in duration), and then reconstructed with independent parameters controlling each grain's onset time, amplitude envelope, and spectral content. The technique enables extreme time-stretching without pitch shift, texture generation from recorded material, and the creation of entirely new timbres through granular density and dispersion control. It was introduced by Iannis Xenakis in the 1970s (notably in the piece DAIS for tape) and persists through digital audio workstations, modular synthesizer patches (Max/MSP, SuperCollider, Pure Data), and dedicated granular synthesis instruments. The persistence mechanism is software implementation and pedagogical tradition in electronic music. [formal: synthetizatio granularis | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Phase vocoder is a signal processing technique for modifying the duration of a signal without changing its pitch. It operates by computing the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) of the signal, manipulating the phase relationships between consecutive frames, and then reconstructing the modified signal via inverse STFT and overlap-add. The key insight is that phase values in consecutive frames follow predictable patterns based on frequency bins; by predicting and adjusting these phase values, the vocoder can stretch or compress time while maintaining coherent pitch. Developed by Joseph Fielder in 1967, it persists through software implementations in audio editing tools (Audacity, Adobe Audition), DAWs, and research code. [formal: vocator phaseum | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Spectral manipulation is a class of signal processing techniques that operate by transforming a signal into its frequency-domain representation (typically via Fourier transform), modifying specific frequency components or spectral characteristics, and then reconstructing a time-domain signal via inverse transform. Common operations include spectral filtering (attenuating or amplifying frequency bands), spectral subtraction (noise estimation and removal), spectral band replication (wideband speech extension), formant shifting (voice transformation), and spectral convolution (reverb synthesis). The technique is foundational in audio processing, telecommunications, image processing, and radar. Its persistence is ensured by the mathematical framework of Fourier analysis and widespread implementation in DSP libraries (librosa, MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox, FFtw-based pipelines). [formal: manipulatio spectralis | substrate: behavior | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.03]

Linear prediction estimates a signal sample as a weighted sum of previous samples: x-hat[n] equals sum of a_k times x[n-k] over prediction order k. The prediction coefficients are computed by minimizing mean squared prediction error, typically via the Yule-Walker equations solved with Levinson-Durbin recursion. The prediction order (number of coefficients) determines model complexity and spectral resolution. Persistence mechanism: encoded in ITU-T speech codecs (G.729, AMR), embedded in audio analysis toolkits (Praat, librosa), formalized in signal processing textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Lyons). [formal: linearis praedictio | substrate: behavior | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Spectral decay measures the rate at which spectral energy decreases over time within an analysis window. It is computed as the time constant of an exponential fit to the energy envelope of successive frequency bins, or equivalently as the difference between early and late spectral energy summed across frames. Parameters include the analysis frame size, window function, frequency bin resolution, and decay fitting method. Persisted through standardized audio analysis algorithms and widely implemented in libraries such as Librosa, Essentia, and MATLAB Signal Processing Toolbox. [formal: decadentia-spectralis | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Pink noise is a class of random signals characterized by a power spectral density that decreases at 3 dB per octave (proportional to 1/frequency), meaning each octave band carries equal acoustic energy. This spectral shape makes pink noise perceptually uniform to human hearing across the audible spectrum. Computed by applying a 1/f filter to white noise or generated via filtered white noise methods. Used in audio system calibration, acoustic measurement, psychoacoustic research, and music production. [formal: rosula | substrate: mind | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

A linear model represents a target variable as a linear combination of predictor variables, weighted by learnable or specified coefficients. The framework takes the form y = Xβ + ε, where X is the design matrix, β the coefficient vector, and ε the error term. It persists through algebraic formulations, computational implementations (OLS, regression solvers), and parametric assumptions about linearity. The model is characterized by its coefficients, design matrix, error structure, and the optimization criterion used to fit it. [formal: model_linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: a life | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Noise cancellation is an audio processing technique that reduces unwanted sound by generating an anti-noise signal. Active noise cancellation uses adaptive filtering to produce a signal that is the phase-inverted copy of the noise; when the two signals combine, destructive interference cancels the noise. The technique operates by (1) sensing the noise via a microphone, (2) processing it through an adaptive filter to produce the anti-phase signal, and (3) outputting the combined signal through a speaker. Passive noise cancellation uses physical barriers and absorption materials to attenuate sound without electronic processing. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic — implemented as DSP routines embedded in hardware (headphones, automotive systems, HVAC) or as software audio filters.[formal: suppressio soni | substrate: behavior | horizon: hours | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.85]

Zero-phase filtering is a technique that eliminates phase distortion by applying a linear filter in both forward and reverse directions. The forward pass imparts phase shift φ(f); the reverse pass imparts −φ(f); the combined transfer function is |H(f)|² with zero net phase. This preserves waveform temporal alignment at the cost of doubled computation and non-causal processing. Parameters: filter H(f), input signal x(n), pass order. Persistence mechanism: the output y(n) retains the input's phase while shaping its magnitude spectrum as |H(f)|².

Spectral magnitude is the absolute value |X(f)| of complex spectral coefficients X(f) at each frequency bin, obtained via Fourier transform or equivalent spectral decomposition of a signal. Parameters: (1) the signal representation (time-domain samples or short-time frames), (2) the spectral decomposition method (DFT, STFT, DCT), (3) normalization convention (raw, dB-scaled, or perceptually weighted). Persistence mechanism: the magnitude spectrum is computed once from the spectral coefficients and stored as a fixed-dimensional vector or function of frequency; subsequent operations (filtering, feature extraction, classification) read this vector without recomputation. Display: Spectral Magnitude — the energy envelope across frequency.

Pre-emphasis is a linear filter that boosts high frequencies, typically implemented as a first-order FIR filter H(z)=1-μz⁻¹ with μ≈0.95-0.97, applied to speech signals before analysis to compensate for natural spectral roll-off and improve high-frequency representation. Parameters: (1) the pre-emphasis coefficient μ; (2) the filter order and implementation domain; (3) the target signal class. Persistence: encoded in speech codecs, audio toolchains, and taught in digital signal processing curricula. [formal: preemphasis | substrate: matter | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.98]

Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies vector spaces, linear transformations, matrices, and systems of linear equations. It provides the formal framework for representing and manipulating linear relationships through abstract algebraic structures. Its core objects — vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, and linear operators — serve as the language for encoding transformations in physics, computer science, engineering, and statistics. The field persists through formal axiomatic systems taught in curricula worldwide and applied in computational libraries.\n\n[formal: algebraa-linearis | substrate: mind | horizon: generations | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.01]

Formant warping is a human-made signal processing operation that nonlinearly maps formant frequencies between source and target vocal tracts to preserve intelligibility in voice conversion and speech synthesis. It is parameterized by a warp factor α and a frequency mapping function W(f) applied to spectral envelopes, typically implemented via filterbank warping or all-pass filter cascades. It persists through coded algorithms in speech toolkits, academic literature, and deployed voice conversion systems.

Formant warp is a human-made signal processing operation that nonlinearly maps formant frequencies between source and target vocal tracts to preserve intelligibility in voice conversion and speech synthesis. Bit-depth is the number of bits used to encode each individual sample value in a digital audio signal. It determines the theoretical maximum dynamic range (approximately 6.02 × N + 1.76 dB for N-bit resolution) and the quantization noise floor (one LSB / √12 for uniform quantization). Standard values are 16-bit (CD quality, 96 dB dynamic range), 24-bit (professional recording, 144 dB dynamic range), and 32-bit float (processing headroom). Key parameters: (1) sample bit-width (integer or floating-point), (2) quantization step size (full-scale range divided by 2^N for integer formats), and (3) encoding scheme (PCM, Delta-Sigma). [formal: profunditas bitium | substrate: digital signal | horizon: audio format specification | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.18]

Bit-depth is a numeric parameter specifying the number of quantization levels used to represent each sample in a digital audio signal.
